laws.title: Constitution of the Republic of Korea 1987
laws.subtitle: Sixth Republic and democratic governance
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's current constitution, adopted in 1987 following pro-democracy protests (the June Democracy Movement), established the Sixth Republic with direct presidential elections. It enshrines fundamental rights, a single five-year presidential term with no re-election, and an independent judiciary with the Constitutional Court. The 2024 impeachment of President Yoon Suk-yeol — following his short-lived declaration of martial law — demonstrated the constitution's accountability mechanisms.
laws.penalty: Constitutional violations adjudicated by Constitutional Court; impeachment for presidents and officials
exceptions: National security emergency provisions
Presidential immunity for official acts (limited)

quiz.q: How long is a South Korean presidential term, and can presidents be re-elected?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's president serves a single five-year term with no possibility of re-election, a provision designed to prevent authoritarian entrenchment after decades of presidential power abuse.

laws.title: National Security Act 1948
laws.subtitle: Anti-communist law and free speech limits
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's National Security Act (NSA) criminalizes activities benefiting North Korea or anti-state organizations, including praising or sympathizing with North Korea, distributing materials deemed to benefit the enemy, and membership in anti-state groups. The NSA has been repeatedly criticized by UN human rights bodies and civil liberties groups as incompatible with international human rights standards. It was used to prosecute labor activists, journalists, and academics during the authoritarian era.
laws.penalty: Up to 7 years imprisonment for NSA violations; death penalty for espionage
exceptions: Academic research on North Korea with approved methodology
Government-authorized North Korea engagement

quiz.q: What does South Korea's National Security Act primarily criminalize?
options: Activities deemed to benefit North Korea
quiz.explanation: South Korea's National Security Act criminalizes activities beneficial to North Korea or anti-state organizations, including praising or sympathizing with the DPRK, distributing certain materials, and membership in designated organizations — provisions widely criticized by human rights groups.

laws.title: Korea's Digital Economy / K-Tech Leadership
laws.subtitle: Semiconductor law and tech regulation
laws.fullDescription: South Korea is a global technology powerhouse — Samsung and SK Hynix control approximately 70% of global DRAM memory production; Samsung leads global NAND flash. The Special Act on National Advanced Strategic Industries (2022) provides massive government support for semiconductors, displays, and batteries. Korea's Digital New Deal and data economy strategies aim to maintain tech leadership against Chinese competition and US CHIPS Act incentives.
laws.penalty: Trade secret theft (especially to China): up to 30 years imprisonment since 2023 reforms
exceptions: Foreign investment in non-strategic tech sectors fully open
Academic technology transfer with government approval
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Trade Industry Energy Korea

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of global DRAM memory production do Samsung and SK Hynix together control?
quiz.explanation: Samsung and SK Hynix together control approximately 70% of global DRAM memory chip production, making South Korea the dominant force in the global semiconductor memory market.

laws.title: Labor Standards Act / Chaebol Labor Relations
laws.subtitle: Worker rights and chaebol dominance
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's Labor Standards Act governs minimum wages, maximum working hours (reduced from 68 to 52 hours/week), and workplace rights. Korea has a dual labor market — regular employees with strong protections and a large precarious irregular worker sector. Chaebol (large family-controlled conglomerates — Samsung, Hyundai, LG, SK) dominate the economy and have had confrontational labor relations. The Korean Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU) is one of Asia's most militant labor federations.
laws.penalty: Labor law violations: fines; repeated violations: criminal prosecution of executives
exceptions: Small employers have modified maximum hours
Special industries (transport, healthcare) have modified rest rules
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Employment and Labor Korea

quiz.q: What is the maximum working hours per week under South Korea's Labor Standards Act (after 2018 reform)?
quiz.explanation: South Korea reformed its working hours law in 2018 to reduce the maximum from 68 to 52 hours per week (40 regular + 12 overtime), aiming to improve work-life balance in one of the OECD's longest-working countries.

laws.title: Military Criminal Act Article 92-6 / Anti-Gay Military Law
laws.subtitle: Criminalization of same-sex acts in military
laws.fullDescription: South Korea criminalizes consensual same-sex sexual activity between male soldiers under Article 92-6 of the Military Criminal Act, with up to 2 years imprisonment. The Constitutional Court upheld this provision in 2023 in a 5-4 decision, despite significant dissent. South Korea has no anti-discrimination law protecting sexual orientation — long-stalled National Human Rights Commission recommendations have not been legislated. Same-sex relationships are not legally recognized.
laws.penalty: Up to 2 years imprisonment for consensual same-sex acts between male soldiers
exceptions: Civilian LGBTQ+ relationships not criminalized (but not recognized)
Military rule applies only within armed forces

quiz.q: What was the Constitutional Court's 2023 ruling on South Korea's military anti-gay law (Article 92-6)?
quiz.explanation: In 2023, South Korea's Constitutional Court upheld Article 92-6 of the Military Criminal Act (criminalizing consensual same-sex acts between soldiers) in a 5-4 decision, disappointing LGBTQ+ rights advocates who had hoped for the provision's repeal.

laws.title: Immigration Control Act / Foreign Workers
laws.subtitle: Migrant workers and multicultural Korea
laws.fullDescription: South Korea faces demographic challenges — among the world's lowest birth rates (0.72 in 2023) — and increasing reliance on migrant workers. The Employment Permit System (EPS) brings in workers from 16 countries. Foreign residents now exceed 2.5 million (5% of population). Korea has been cautious about immigration amid social tensions — anti-immigrant sentiment is growing. The government has increased immigration targets to address labor shortages.
laws.penalty: Overstaying visa: deportation; unauthorized work: criminal penalties for employers
exceptions: Ethnic Korean returnees (overseas Koreans) have privileged status
Refugees receive limited protections

quiz.q: What was South Korea's total fertility rate in 2023 — one of the world's lowest?
quiz.explanation: South Korea recorded a total fertility rate of just 0.72 in 2023 — the world's lowest — a demographic crisis that is driving increased immigration, significant policy attention, and concern about economic sustainability.

laws.title: Broadcasting Act / JTBC and Media Landscape
laws.subtitle: Press freedom and media regulation
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has a vibrant but politically polarized media landscape — major broadcasters KBS, MBC, and SBS, plus cable news channels (JTBC, YTN, MBN). JTBC's 2016 reporting on the Choi Soon-sil scandal that led to President Park Geun-hye's impeachment demonstrated investigative journalism's power. Korea ranks around 62nd globally on press freedom (RSF), with concerns about concentration of media ownership and advertiser pressure on editorial independence.
laws.penalty: Criminal defamation (including online defamation): up to 2 years imprisonment — controversial provision
exceptions: Truth is a defense in criminal defamation
Public interest journalism protection

quiz.q: Which South Korean broadcaster's investigative journalism in 2016 exposed the scandal leading to President Park Geun-hye's impeachment?
quiz.explanation: JTBC (a cable news channel) was instrumental in the 2016 exposé of the Choi Soon-sil scandal — reporting that Park Geun-hye's confidante had accessed and edited presidential speeches — that triggered the impeachment process.

laws.title: Choi Soon-sil / Park Geun-hye Impeachment
laws.subtitle: Anti-corruption and chaebol accountability
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has had multiple presidential corruption scandals — Park Geun-hye was impeached (2016) and imprisoned for bribery, coercion, and abuse of power in the Choi Soon-sil influence-peddling scandal. Lee Myung-bak was imprisoned for bribery. The Kim Young Ran Act (Anti-Corruption Act 2016) limits gifts and entertainment for public officials, journalists, and academics. Chaebol executives have frequently faced prosecution but have often received pardons from subsequent administrations.
laws.penalty: Bribery: up to life imprisonment; Kim Young Ran Act violations: up to 3 years
exceptions: Presidential pardon power has been used extensively for chaebol executives
Whistleblower protections under Anti-Corruption Act
laws.sourceLabel: Anti-Corruption and Civil Rights Commission Korea

quiz.q: What is the Kim Young Ran Act (2016) designed to prevent?
options: Excessive gifts and entertainment to public officials, journalists, and academics
quiz.explanation: The Kim Young Ran Act (Anti-Corruption Act 2016) limits the value of gifts, meals, and entertainment that can be given to public officials, journalists, and educators — targeting the hospitality culture that had facilitated corruption.

laws.title: Chaebol Reform / Fair Trade Act
laws.subtitle: Korea Fair Trade Commission and conglomerate regulation
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's economy is dominated by chaebols — Samsung, Hyundai, LG, SK, Lotte — family-controlled conglomerates. The Korea Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) regulates chaebols under the Monopoly Regulation and Fair Trade Act, restricting cross-shareholding and requiring governance improvements. The 'Korea Discount' — where Korean companies trade at lower valuations than global peers — has been attributed to poor governance, low dividends, and cross-shareholding opacity.
laws.penalty: KFTC fines; criminal referral for serious antitrust violations
exceptions: Holding company structure permitted under KFTC rules
SME cooperation agreements exempted

quiz.q: What term describes the phenomenon of Korean companies trading at lower valuations than global peers?
quiz.explanation: The 'Korea Discount' refers to the phenomenon where Korean listed companies trade at significantly lower price-to-earnings multiples than comparable companies in other markets, attributed to poor corporate governance, low shareholder returns, and complex cross-shareholding structures.

laws.title: Martial Law Declaration 2024 / Yoon Impeachment
laws.subtitle: Constitutional crisis and presidential accountability
laws.fullDescription: President Yoon Suk-yeol declared martial law on 3 December 2024 — the first since 1980 — claiming opposition-controlled parliamentary 'anti-state activities'. The National Assembly voted to lift martial law within 6 hours. Yoon was impeached by the National Assembly in December 2024, arrested in January 2025, and faced trial for insurrection. The Constitutional Court sustained the impeachment in April 2025. The episode demonstrated Korea's democratic resilience.
laws.penalty: Insurrection carries death penalty or life imprisonment under Korean law
exceptions: Constitutional emergency powers exist but require parliamentary check
Acting president assumes duties pending Constitutional Court ruling

quiz.q: How long did Yoon Suk-yeol's martial law declaration last before the National Assembly voted to lift it?
quiz.explanation: President Yoon's 3 December 2024 martial law declaration lasted approximately 6 hours before the National Assembly voted 190-0 to lift it, with MPs physically breaking into the barricaded parliament to cast their votes.

laws.title: Education Act / Hagwon and Academic Pressure
laws.subtitle: Private tutoring and education fever
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's education system is globally renowned for academic achievement but criticized for extreme pressure. The college entrance exam (CSAT/Suneung) determines university placement and life outcomes. Hagwons (private tutoring academies) are a massive industry — Seoul banned hagwons after 10pm to reduce academic pressure. The government periodically attempts to reduce private tutoring costs. Korea's education paradox: globally highest results but high youth suicide rates partly linked to academic pressure.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed hagwon operation: fines; operating after curfew: sanctions
exceptions: Foreign language instruction has modified rules
Online tutoring has different regulations

quiz.q: What is the name of South Korea's all-important national college entrance exam?
quiz.explanation: The CSAT (College Scholastic Ability Test), known in Korean as the Suneung, is South Korea's national college entrance examination, taken annually in November. Its results largely determine university admission and have enormous life consequences.

laws.title: National Health Insurance Act / NHIS
laws.subtitle: Universal healthcare and medical system
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's National Health Insurance system, managed by the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS), provides near-universal coverage (97%+ of population). Premium-based contributions from employers and employees fund coverage. South Korea has one of the world's most advanced healthcare systems — high physician density, sophisticated technology, and very affordable costs. Medical tourism attracts patients from China, Southeast Asia, and beyond. K-beauty and plastic surgery are significant sectors.
laws.penalty: Healthcare fraud: criminal prosecution; NHIS can claim recovery with penalties
exceptions: Most dental and optometry services require supplemental insurance
Cosmetic procedures not covered

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of South Korea's population is covered by the National Health Insurance system?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's National Health Insurance system covers over 97% of the population, providing near-universal health coverage and making South Korea one of the most successful countries in achieving universal healthcare.

laws.title: Gender Pay Gap / Feminism and Anti-Feminism
laws.subtitle: Korea's gender equality debates
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has one of the OECD's largest gender pay gaps (~31%) and lowest female labor force participation rates among advanced economies. The country is polarized on gender issues — the 4B movement (women eschewing marriage, dating, sex, childbirth) emerged as a feminist response to gender-based violence and discrimination. Anti-feminist sentiment, particularly among young men ('incel' culture), has become a political factor. The Ministry of Gender Equality and Family has faced calls for abolition from conservative politicians.
laws.penalty: Workplace gender discrimination: Labor Rights Commission remedies; sexual harassment: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Military service exemption for women is one of few formal gender distinctions
Women-only spaces protected under anti-discrimination framework

quiz.q: What is the '4B movement' in South Korea?
options: A feminist movement rejecting marriage, dating, sex, and childbirth
quiz.explanation: The 4B movement ('bihon, bichulsan, biyeonae, bisekseu') is a South Korean feminist movement where women reject marriage, childbirth, dating, and heterosexual sex as a protest against gender discrimination, patriarchal expectations, and gender-based violence.

laws.title: Personal Information Protection Act / PIPA
laws.subtitle: Data protection and digital privacy
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA), significantly revised in 2023, is one of Asia's most comprehensive data protection laws, with principles similar to GDPR. The Personal Information Protection Commission (PIPC) is the independent enforcement authority. Korea has among the world's highest smartphone penetration and digital services usage. Korea Mobile ID (PASS) and various biometric authentication systems raise privacy questions.
laws.penalty: PIPA violations: fines up to 3% of turnover; criminal prosecution for intentional violations
exceptions: Public benefit research has modified consent requirements
National security and law enforcement exemptions

quiz.q: What EU law is South Korea's PIPA (Personal Information Protection Act) most commonly compared to?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) is frequently compared to the EU's GDPR (General Data Protection Regulation), as both establish comprehensive data protection frameworks with similar principles around consent, data subjects' rights, and regulatory oversight.

laws.title: Korean War Armistice / North Korea Threat
laws.subtitle: Unification policy and DMZ
laws.fullDescription: South Korea remains technically at war with North Korea — the 1950-53 Korean War ended with an armistice, not a peace treaty. The DMZ (Demilitarized Zone) is one of the world's most militarized borders. All Korean men must complete 18-21 months of mandatory military service. North Korea's nuclear program (ICBM tests, nuclear tests) poses an existential threat. The ROK-US Combined Forces Command provides the core defense alliance.
laws.penalty: Desertion from mandatory military service: up to 3 years imprisonment
exceptions: Conscientious objectors served prison time until 2018 (now alternative service available)
Religious exemptions not granted — alternative civil service only

quiz.q: What type of legal document ended the Korean War in 1953?
quiz.explanation: The Korean War ended in 1953 with an armistice agreement (ceasefire), not a formal peace treaty. This means South and North Korea remain technically in a state of war, making the Korean peninsula one of the world's most enduring unresolved conflicts.

laws.title: Cybercrime Law / Digital Sex Crime Act
laws.subtitle: Digital sex crimes and revenge porn
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has severe problems with digital sex crimes — non-consensual filming (hidden cameras/molka) and distribution of intimate images. The 2020 N번방 (Nth Room Case) — a Telegram-based network distributing filmed sexual abuse of women and minors — led to life sentences for perpetrators and legislative reform. The Act on Special Cases in Punishment of Sexual Crimes strengthened penalties significantly. Korea's pervasive CCTV and digital surveillance create both safety and privacy tensions.
laws.penalty: Non-consensual filming: up to 7 years; distribution of filmed sexual abuse: up to 10 years
exceptions: Legitimate security cameras with disclosure
Law enforcement recording under warrant
laws.sourceLabel: Korea Digital Sex Crime Victim Support Center

quiz.q: What 2020 case involving Telegram channels distributing filmed sexual abuse led to major reforms of South Korea's digital sex crime laws?
quiz.explanation: The N번방 (Nth Room Case) was a 2020 Korean case where criminal networks used Telegram to distribute filmed sexual abuse of women and minors, extorted victims into producing more material, and charged subscribers. It led to life sentences and major legislative reform.

laws.title: 2050 Carbon Neutrality Act / Green New Deal
laws.subtitle: Climate policy and renewable transition
laws.fullDescription: South Korea, the world's 10th largest carbon emitter, passed the Carbon Neutrality Act 2021, targeting 40% emissions reduction by 2030 and carbon neutrality by 2050. Korea's Korean Green New Deal allocates 73.4 trillion won (~$63 billion) for green infrastructure, electric vehicles, and renewable energy. Korea is a major manufacturer of EV batteries (LG, Samsung SDI, SK Innovation). However, Korea is also a major coal power user and exporter of coal finance.
laws.penalty: Carbon market compliance fines; emissions permit violations: regulatory sanctions
exceptions: Heavy industry transition allowances
Export credit agency coal finance phase-out timeline

quiz.q: What emissions reduction target has South Korea set for 2030 under its Carbon Neutrality Act?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's Carbon Neutrality Act 2021 sets a nationally determined contribution (NDC) of 40% emissions reduction from 2018 levels by 2030, and carbon neutrality by 2050.

laws.title: Korea-US FTA (KORUS) and Trade Policy
laws.subtitle: Trade agreements and export economy
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's export-driven economy depends heavily on free trade — exports account for about 40% of GDP. The KORUS FTA (2012) was one of the largest US trade deals outside NAFTA. South Korea has FTAs with the EU, ASEAN, China, UK, and others. Korea is heavily integrated into global semiconductor and automotive supply chains. US tariffs on Korean steel and cars under Section 232 created tensions. Korea joined IPEF (Indo-Pacific Economic Framework).
laws.penalty: Customs violations: significant fines and criminal prosecution
exceptions: KORUS rules of origin requirements for preferential tariffs
Defense-related procurement has national security carve-outs

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of South Korea's GDP does exports account for?
quiz.explanation: Exports account for approximately 40% of South Korea's GDP, making it one of the world's most export-dependent major economies and highly sensitive to global trade policy, tariffs, and supply chain disruptions.

laws.title: Real Estate Speculation Control / Lease Law
laws.subtitle: Jeonse system and housing affordability
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's unique Jeonse system — where tenants pay a large lump sum deposit (50-80% of property value) instead of monthly rent, earning the landlord investment returns — became a crisis when interest rates rose and property values fell in 2022-23, with some landlords unable to return deposits. The government tightened regulations on Jeonse after widespread fraud ('Jeonse scams'). Seoul has among Asia's highest property prices relative to income.
laws.penalty: Jeonse deposit fraud: criminal prosecution; landlord failure to return: civil enforcement
exceptions: Short-term rentals (Wolse, monthly rent) have different rules
Government-subsidized housing has different deposit rules
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Land Infrastructure Transport Korea

quiz.q: What is the unique Korean rental system where tenants pay a large lump-sum deposit instead of monthly rent?
quiz.explanation: Jeonse is a uniquely Korean rental system where tenants pay a large lump-sum deposit (typically 50-80% of property value) to the landlord instead of monthly rent, with the deposit returned in full at the end of the lease period.

laws.title: Population Crisis Policy / Pro-Natalist Incentives
laws.subtitle: Birth rate crisis and family policy
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's fertility rate of 0.72 (2023) — the world's lowest — has prompted emergency measures: increased childcare subsidies, parental leave expansion (paid maternity 90 days, paternity 10 days), cash payments for newborns, and housing benefits for families. Despite spending over $200 billion on pro-natalist policies since 2006, birth rates have continued to fall. The causes — extreme housing costs, education pressure, gender inequality, and long working hours — are deep structural issues.
laws.penalty: No penalties related to childbearing; incentives only
exceptions: Foreign-born children in Korea have different citizenship rules
Adoption law recently reformed to increase domestic adoption
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Health and Welfare Korea

quiz.q: Approximately how much has South Korea spent on pro-natalist policies since 2006?
quiz.explanation: South Korea has spent over $200 billion on pro-natalist policies since 2006, making it one of the world's most expensive birth rate promotion programs — yet fertility rates have continued to fall to historic lows.

laws.title: Stalking Prevention Act 2021
laws.subtitle: Stalking criminalization and victim protection
laws.fullDescription: South Korea criminalized stalking in 2021 after years of advocacy following numerous femicide cases where victims had reported stalkers without legal protection. The Stalking Crimes Punishment Act 2021 makes stalking a criminal offense with up to 3 years imprisonment (5 years if weapons involved). Emergency restraining orders can be issued immediately. Korea had a notable 2021 case where a stalking victim was murdered in a subway station just after filing a complaint.
laws.penalty: Stalking offense: up to 3 years imprisonment; armed stalking: up to 5 years
exceptions: Police can issue emergency measures without arrest immediately
Repeat violations trigger mandatory detention
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Gender Equality Korea Stalking

quiz.q: In what year did South Korea criminalize stalking with the Stalking Crimes Punishment Act?
quiz.explanation: South Korea criminalized stalking in 2021 with the Stalking Crimes Punishment Act, after years of advocacy following multiple femicide cases where victims had reported stalkers to police but received little legal protection.

laws.title: Public Official Election Act / Political Funding
laws.subtitle: Election law and campaign finance
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's Public Official Election Act strictly regulates campaigns — election periods, campaign activities, and political financing are tightly controlled. The National Election Commission (NEC) oversees elections. Political parties (PPP and DP as major parties) rely on government funding. Korea uses a combination of constituency-based and proportional representation for the National Assembly. The 2024 general election saw the opposition Democratic Party win a landslide despite Yoon's presidency.
laws.penalty: Election law violations: criminal prosecution; illegal campaign financing: imprisonment up to 5 years
exceptions: Incumbents have modified campaign activity rules
Political party internal elections have modified rules

quiz.q: What body oversees elections in South Korea?
quiz.explanation: The National Election Commission (NEC) is the independent constitutional body that oversees elections, political parties, and campaign finance in South Korea, operating independently from the government.

laws.title: National Tax Service / Corporate Tax
laws.subtitle: Korean tax system and chaebols
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's National Tax Service (NTS) administers income tax (top rate 45%), corporate tax (top rate 24%), and VAT (10%). Korea has a comprehensive tax treaty network. Chaebol tax planning — through holding companies, family foundations, and intragroup transactions — has been a major focus of tax enforcement. The inheritance tax rate reaches 60% (maximum for largest inheritances), which chaebol families have tried to minimize through various structures.
laws.penalty: Tax evasion: up to 10 years imprisonment; civil penalties up to 40% of evaded tax
exceptions: SME tax incentives are extensive
R&D tax credits for qualifying technology investment

quiz.q: What is South Korea's maximum inheritance tax rate, one of the world's highest?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's maximum inheritance tax rate reaches 60% (50% base plus 10% surtax for the largest inheritances by controlling shareholders), one of the world's highest, making inheritance planning a major concern for Korea's chaebol families.

laws.title: E-commerce Law / Platform Economy
laws.subtitle: Online retail and consumer rights
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has one of the world's most advanced e-commerce ecosystems — Coupang (the 'Amazon of Korea') processes millions of deliveries daily with same-day delivery. The Act on Consumer Protection in Electronic Commerce governs online sales, subscription services, and digital platforms. Kakao and Naver dominate digital commerce, messaging, and payments. Korea's 'super apps' integrate payments, shopping, and social media. Digital consumer fraud prosecution has increased.
laws.penalty: E-commerce consumer fraud: criminal prosecution; false advertising: KFTC sanctions
exceptions: B2B digital transactions have reduced consumer law protections
International cross-border purchases have modified rules

quiz.q: What South Korean e-commerce company is often called the 'Amazon of Korea'?
quiz.explanation: Coupang is often called the 'Amazon of Korea' due to its dominant market position, Rocket Delivery same-day service, and integrated logistics network that has transformed South Korean e-commerce.

laws.title: Criminal Defamation / Press Law
laws.subtitle: Defamation and media freedom
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has criminal defamation laws — including a provision (Article 310 of Criminal Act) making even true statements defamatory if published with intent to harm reputation. This provision has been used against journalists reporting on public figures. Korea ranks around 62nd on the RSF Press Freedom Index. The Korea Communications Standards Commission (KCSC) can order removal of online content. The Yoon government used defamation law against critical media more aggressively than predecessors.
laws.penalty: Criminal defamation with true facts: up to 2 years; false facts: up to 5 years
exceptions: Truthful statements in public interest are protected
Parliamentary privilege for assembly statements

quiz.q: What is unusual about South Korea's criminal defamation law compared to most democracies?
options: Truth is not always a complete defense — true statements can still be defamatory
It only applies to online speech
quiz.explanation: Unusually among democracies, South Korea's criminal defamation law (Article 310 of the Criminal Act) makes even true statements defamatory if published with intent to harm reputation, unlike most legal systems where truth is an absolute defense.

laws.title: New Town Development / Greenbelt Policy
laws.subtitle: Urban planning and land use
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's urban planning includes strict greenbelt zones around major cities — protected from development since the 1970s — and large-scale New Town developments (Bundang, Ilsan, Pangyo) to accommodate Seoul's enormous population. The Capital Region Relocation Policy moved government agencies to the new administrative capital Sejong. Seoul's metropolitan area houses half of Korea's 51 million population.
laws.penalty: Greenbelt violations: criminal prosecution; unauthorized construction: demolition orders
exceptions: Agricultural activities permitted within greenbelt
Public facilities (schools, parks) allowed in greenbelt

quiz.q: Approximately what percentage of South Korea's 51 million population lives in the Seoul metropolitan area?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 50% of South Korea's 51 million population lives in the Seoul Capital Area (Seoul, Incheon, Gyeonggi Province), making it one of the world's most concentrated urban agglomerations relative to national population.

laws.title: Bioethics and Safety Act / Human Cloning
laws.subtitle: Bioethics and medical research law
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's Bioethics and Safety Act (2004, substantially revised) governs embryonic research, genetic testing, and biomedical research. Korea was involved in a major scientific fraud when Hwang Woo-suk's claimed stem cell breakthroughs (2004-2005) were found to be fabricated. Despite the scandal, Korea has rebuilt credibility in biomedical research. Pharmaceutical manufacturing and medical devices are major export industries (COVID-19 test kit exports were a success story).
laws.penalty: Illegal human cloning: up to 10 years imprisonment; unauthorized genetic testing: fines
exceptions: Therapeutic cloning (nuclear transfer) allowed under strict conditions
Prenatal genetic testing with consent

quiz.q: What major scientific fraud involving South Korea was exposed in 2005?
options: Hwang Woo-suk's fabricated stem cell research claims
quiz.explanation: In 2005, South Korean scientist Hwang Woo-suk's landmark claims of creating human embryonic stem cell lines through therapeutic cloning (published in Science) were found to be entirely fabricated, in one of the largest scientific fraud cases in history.

laws.title: National Pension Service / Aging Society
laws.subtitle: NPS and retirement funding
laws.fullDescription: The National Pension Service (NPS) manages Korea's public pension — one of the world's largest pension funds at over $800 billion. With Korea's ultra-low birth rate (0.72 in 2023), the NPS is projected to be depleted by 2055. Pension reform — increasing contributions, reducing benefits, or raising retirement age — is one of Korea's most politically contentious issues. The Yoon government proposed reforms in 2024 that Parliament debated extensively.
laws.penalty: NPS contribution evasion: civil penalties; employers failing to register workers: criminal sanctions
exceptions: Self-employed have separate premium rules
Low income workers receive premium subsidies

quiz.q: Approximately how large is South Korea's National Pension Service (NPS) fund?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's National Pension Service (NPS) manages over $800 billion in assets, making it one of the world's largest pension funds, though it faces long-term sustainability challenges due to Korea's ultra-low birth rate.

laws.title: K-Content Export Law / Hallyu Wave
laws.subtitle: Korean Wave and cultural soft power
laws.fullDescription: The Korean Wave (Hallyu) — encompassing K-pop (BTS, BLACKPINK), K-dramas, K-movies (Parasite's 2020 Oscar win), and K-food — is a major cultural and economic phenomenon. The Content Industry Promotion Act and Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism support Korean content exports. K-pop companies (HYBE, SM, YG, JYP) operate under intense artist management systems that have faced scrutiny for exploitative contracts. BTS's global success prompted discussion of military service exemptions for cultural contributors.
laws.penalty: Intellectual property violations: criminal prosecution; illegal content distribution: significant fines
exceptions: Fair use in educational contexts
Parody and criticism protected under some conditions
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Culture Sports Tourism Korea

quiz.q: Which South Korean film became the first non-English-language film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture?
quiz.explanation: Parasite (2019), directed by Bong Joon-ho, became the first non-English-language film to win the Academy Award for Best Picture at the 2020 Oscars, a historic achievement for South Korean cinema and global cinema generally.

laws.title: Anti-Discrimination Act Debate
laws.subtitle: Long-stalled comprehensive equality law
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has been debating a comprehensive anti-discrimination act since 2007. Sixteen attempts to pass such legislation have failed, blocked primarily by opposition from conservative Christian groups who oppose protection for sexual orientation and gender identity. The National Human Rights Commission has repeatedly called for the law. Without it, discrimination on grounds of sexual orientation, age, disability in many contexts lacks specific legal remedy.
laws.penalty: Currently no comprehensive anti-discrimination law — discrimination addressed piecemeal under specific laws
exceptions: Disability discrimination: Disability Discrimination Prohibition Act (2007) provides some protection
Employment discrimination: Labor Standards Act provides limited protection

quiz.q: How many times has South Korea attempted to pass a comprehensive anti-discrimination act since 2007?
quiz.explanation: South Korea has made approximately sixteen legislative attempts to pass a comprehensive anti-discrimination act since 2007, all failing primarily due to opposition from conservative religious groups opposed to including protection for sexual orientation and gender identity.

laws.title: AI Framework / Robot Ethics
laws.subtitle: Artificial intelligence and digital regulation
laws.fullDescription: South Korea is a global leader in AI and robotics. The Intelligent Robotics Development and Distribution Promotion Act (2008) was one of the world's first robot laws. Samsung and LG are major AI hardware producers. Korea established an AI Policy Framework and joined the Bletchley AI Safety Declaration (2023). Deepfakes and AI-generated intimate images — prevalent in Korea — have driven specific criminal legislation. Korea's data center infrastructure underpins Asia's AI development.
laws.penalty: AI-generated deepfake sexual content: up to 5 years imprisonment (2024 reform)
exceptions: AI in healthcare requires MFDS approval
Research and development exceptions under AI promotion law
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Science and ICT Korea

quiz.q: What 2008 Korean legislation was notable for being among the world's first dedicated robot laws?
options: Intelligent Robotics Development and Distribution Promotion Act 2008
quiz.explanation: South Korea's Intelligent Robotics Development and Distribution Promotion Act (2008) was one of the world's first dedicated pieces of legislation governing the development and deployment of intelligent robots, reflecting Korea's early commitment to robotics as a strategic industry.

laws.title: Narcotic Drugs Control Act
laws.subtitle: Drug policy and zero tolerance
laws.fullDescription: South Korea takes a strict zero-tolerance approach to drugs. Even personal use of cannabis abroad by Korean citizens can result in prosecution upon return to Korea. Random drug testing can be ordered by police. High-profile celebrity drug arrests are heavily publicized. Methamphetamine ('philopon') is the dominant drug problem. Korea has some of the world's strictest penalties for drug offenses, with life imprisonment possible for large-scale trafficking.
laws.penalty: Cannabis personal use: up to 5 years; trafficking: life imprisonment possible
exceptions: Medical cannabis very limited in scope
Authorized research use
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Food and Drug Safety Korea

quiz.q: What is the Korean name for methamphetamine, South Korea's most prevalent illicit drug?
quiz.explanation: Philopon (필로폰) is the Korean term for methamphetamine, which is the most prevalent illegal drug in South Korea. Despite strict enforcement, demand has persisted especially in certain demographic groups.

laws.title: THAAD Deployment / US Alliance Law
laws.subtitle: ROK-US alliance and missile defense
laws.fullDescription: The deployment of the US Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system in South Korea in 2017 triggered significant Chinese economic retaliation — restrictions on K-pop, Korean tourism in China, and discrimination against Lotte (which provided the land). The ROK-US Mutual Defense Treaty (1953) underpins the security alliance. Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) governing US military personnel in Korea has been periodically controversial.
laws.penalty: SOFA violations: US military justice system; criminal offenses against Koreans: complex jurisdiction questions
exceptions: US military personnel have some SOFA jurisdictional protections
SOFA reforms have transferred some jurisdiction to Korean courts

quiz.q: Which US missile defense system deployed in South Korea in 2017 triggered Chinese economic retaliation?
quiz.explanation: The deployment of the US THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) missile defense system at a Lotte Golf Club site in 2017 triggered significant Chinese economic retaliation against South Korea, including boycotts, restrictions on Korean tourism, and discrimination against Korean businesses in China.

laws.title: Basic Livelihood Security Act / Social Safety Net
laws.subtitle: Welfare system and poverty policy
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's Basic Livelihood Security Act (2000) provides a minimum standard of living guarantee. Korea has rapidly developed from one of the world's poorest countries (1960s) to a high-income OECD member in two generations. However, relative poverty among the elderly is severe — over 40% of those 65+ live in relative poverty, one of the OECD's highest rates. The Earned Income Tax Credit (EITC) supplements income for low-income workers.
laws.penalty: Welfare fraud: repayment and criminal prosecution
exceptions: Disabled persons receive enhanced benefits
Single-parent households have modified eligibility
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Health and Welfare Korea Welfare

quiz.q: What percentage of South Koreans aged 65+ live in relative poverty — one of the OECD's highest rates?
quiz.explanation: Over 40% of South Koreans aged 65 and over live in relative poverty, one of the highest rates in the OECD, reflecting inadequate public pension coverage for generations who worked during Korea's industrial development era without pension systems.

laws.title: Civil Act 1958 / Family Law Reform
laws.subtitle: Civil code and family law modernization
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's Civil Act 1958 covers contracts, property, and family law. Significant reforms include abolition of the Hoju (family head) system in 2008, which had embedded patriarchal family structure in law. Adoption law was reformed (2012) requiring court approval rather than private arrangement. Divorce law — both by agreement and contested — is governed by the Family Court. Korea's Supreme Court has expanded inheritance rights and marriage property rules.
laws.penalty: Contract violations: civil damages; family law violations: family court orders
exceptions: Customary practices recognized in some inheritance matters
International family law under Hague Convention

quiz.q: What patriarchal family registration system did South Korea abolish in 2008?
quiz.explanation: South Korea abolished the Hoju (family head) system in 2008, which had registered all family members under the name of the male head of household, reflecting and reinforcing patriarchal family structures. Replaced by an individual-based family registration system.

laws.title: Financial Supervisory Service / Banking Regulation
laws.subtitle: FSS and Korea's financial sector
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's financial system is regulated by the Financial Services Commission (FSC, policy) and Financial Supervisory Service (FSS, examination). Korea's major banks include KB, Shinhan, Hana, and Woori. Korea experienced severe financial crisis during the 1997 Asian Financial Crisis — the IMF bailout came with painful structural reforms. Korea has since built substantial foreign exchange reserves ($400 billion+) as insurance against currency crises. Kakao Bank and Toss are leading digital banks.
laws.penalty: Banking law violations: regulatory sanctions; financial fraud: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Internet-only banks have modified capital requirements
Fintech sandbox allows innovation with modified rules

quiz.q: What event in 1997 forced South Korea to accept an IMF bailout and implement painful structural economic reforms?
quiz.explanation: The 1997 Asian Financial Crisis severely hit South Korea, requiring an IMF bailout of $57 billion — then the largest ever — accompanied by painful restructuring of banks and chaebols, and mass layoffs. The experience led Korea to build large foreign exchange reserves as a safeguard.

laws.title: Corruption — SK Hynix, Samsung Prosecutions
laws.subtitle: Chaebol prosecution history
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has a pattern of prosecuting chaebol leaders for corruption, followed by pardons. Samsung's Lee Jae-yong was convicted of bribery in the Park Geun-hye scandal (2017), imprisoned, released, re-tried, and ultimately pardoned. SK Group's Chey Tae-won was imprisoned for embezzlement. Hyundai's Chung Mong-koo was convicted. Critics point to a revolving door of prosecution and pardon as evidence that powerful interests are not truly held accountable.
laws.penalty: Chaebol bribery: imprisonment; asset confiscation
exceptions: Presidential pardon power used repeatedly for chaebol executives
'Economic necessity' defense has informally influenced pardons

quiz.q: Which chaebol heir was convicted of bribery in connection with the Park Geun-hye scandal and later pardoned?
quiz.explanation: Samsung heir Lee Jae-yong was convicted of bribery in connection with the Park Geun-hye influence-peddling scandal, imprisoned, released on parole, re-tried, and ultimately pardoned — exemplifying the pattern of chaebol prosecution followed by pardon in South Korea.

laws.title: Mental Health Welfare Act / Suicide Prevention
laws.subtitle: Mental health and Korea's suicide rate
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has one of the OECD's highest suicide rates — approximately 24 per 100,000 (2023), with suicide being the leading cause of death for Koreans aged 10-39. The Mental Health Welfare Act governs mental health services. The government's Suicide Prevention Action Plan includes media reporting guidelines (Werther effect concerns). Elderly poverty, youth academic pressure, and social isolation are key drivers. Korea has invested in community mental health centers.
laws.penalty: Criminal liability for encouraging suicide: up to 1 year imprisonment
exceptions: Suicide prevention hotlines have different privacy rules
Mental health involuntary admission requires court review
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Health Welfare Korea Mental Health

quiz.q: What is the leading cause of death for South Koreans aged 10-39?
quiz.explanation: Suicide is the leading cause of death for South Koreans aged 10-39, with South Korea having one of the OECD's highest suicide rates at approximately 24 per 100,000 people annually, driven by academic pressure, elderly poverty, and social isolation.

laws.title: Network Act / Internet Real-Name System
laws.subtitle: Internet identity and censorship
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has experimented with internet real-name requirements — briefly required from 2007-2012 before the Constitutional Court struck it down as unconstitutional. Korea has one of the world's highest internet penetration rates. The Korea Communications Standards Commission (KCSC) can order blocking of websites — gambling, gambling sites, and North Korean propaganda sites are regularly blocked. Social media platforms must comply with KCSC content removal orders.
laws.penalty: Operating blocked services: criminal prosecution; non-compliance with KCSC orders: fines
exceptions: VPN use is not explicitly illegal (though platforms are blocked)
Academic access to some blocked content with authorization

quiz.q: What happened to South Korea's internet real-name system in 2012?
options: It was struck down as unconstitutional by the Constitutional Court
It was extended to all platforms
quiz.explanation: South Korea's internet real-name verification system (requiring users to verify identity before posting online), introduced in 2007, was struck down by the Constitutional Court in 2012 as an unconstitutional violation of freedom of expression and privacy.

laws.title: Constitutional Court / Judicial Review
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Court decisions and democracy
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's Constitutional Court (established 1988) has been central to democratic governance, ruling on constitutional disputes, individual rights petitions, and impeachment trials. Landmark decisions include: overturning the internet real-name system (2012), unanimously dissolving the pro-North Korean Unified Progressive Party (2014), and ruling on Yoon's impeachment (2025). The Court has generally expanded civil liberties and maintained democratic guardrails.
laws.penalty: Constitutional Court orders are binding on all branches; violations can trigger further legal proceedings
exceptions: Court cannot rule on political questions
Emergency powers have some limits on judicial review

quiz.q: In 2014, South Korea's Constitutional Court took what historic action regarding the Unified Progressive Party?
quiz.explanation: In December 2014, South Korea's Constitutional Court unanimously dissolved the Unified Progressive Party (UPP), finding it had a hidden agenda to establish a North Korean-style socialist system in South Korea — the first time a political party had been dissolved in Korea's constitutional history.

laws.title: Fine Dust Special Act / Air Quality
laws.subtitle: Air pollution and China relations
laws.fullDescription: South Korea suffers severe air pollution — particularly PM2.5 fine dust — with significant Chinese cross-border contributions. The Special Act on the Improvement of Air Quality in Seoul Metropolitan Area and the Fine Dust Management Special Act impose restrictions on diesel vehicles, industrial emissions, and coal plants during high-pollution periods. South Korea and China have cooperated (somewhat) on joint weather-modification cloud seeding and dust forecasting.
laws.penalty: Emission standard violations: significant fines; emergency closure orders for high-pollution industries
exceptions: Emergency power plants may temporarily exceed limits
Agricultural burning with permits
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Environment Korea Air Quality

quiz.q: What is the Korean term for the severe air pollution (particularly fine dust/PM2.5) that regularly blankets the country?
quiz.explanation: Misemeonji (미세먼지) is the Korean term for fine dust (PM2.5 and PM10) particles that cause severe air pollution in South Korea, often worsened by yellow dust (hwangsa) blowing from China and Mongolia.

laws.title: Road Traffic Act / Drunk Driving Crackdown
laws.subtitle: DUI law and road safety
laws.fullDescription: South Korea significantly tightened its drunk driving laws with the 'Yoon Chang-ho law' (2019), named after a police officer killed by a drunk driver. The blood alcohol limit was lowered from 0.05% to 0.03%, and penalties increased substantially — license revocation now occurs at 0.03%, and criminal prosecution at 0.08%. South Korea's traffic fatality rate has declined significantly with stricter enforcement.
laws.penalty: Driving at 0.03% BAC: license suspension; over 0.08%: criminal prosecution up to 5 years
exceptions: Zero tolerance for commercial drivers
Repeat offenses: mandatory imprisonment

quiz.q: What is the blood alcohol limit in South Korea for license revocation after the 2019 'Yoon Chang-ho Law' reform?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's 'Yoon Chang-ho Law' (2019) lowered the drunk driving threshold for license revocation to 0.03% BAC (from 0.05%), and the criminal prosecution threshold to 0.08%, in response to a tragic case where a police officer was killed by a repeat drunk driver.

laws.title: Disability Act / Welfare of Persons with Disabilities
laws.subtitle: Disability rights and accessibility
laws.fullDescription: The Act on Welfare of Persons with Disabilities (1989, revised 2007) and the Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination Against Disabled Persons (2007) provide the legal framework for disability rights in Korea. Korea has made significant progress in subway accessibility (lawsuits by disability rights activists), but enforcement of reasonable accommodation in employment and service access remains inconsistent. Disability activist group protests have disrupted subway service to draw attention to rights gaps.
laws.penalty: Disability discrimination in employment: remedies via Labor Commission; service access: complaints to NHRC
exceptions: Reasonable accommodation has proportionality considerations
Small businesses have modified obligations
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Health Welfare Disability Korea

quiz.q: What tactic have Korean disability rights activists used to draw attention to accessibility demands?
options: Subway service disruptions during rush hour
quiz.explanation: Korean disability rights activists, particularly the group SADD (Solidarity Against Disability Discrimination), have disrupted subway services during rush hours to draw public and government attention to demands for better mobility access and disability welfare funding.

laws.title: Industrial Espionage / Trade Secret Law
laws.subtitle: Technology theft and national security
laws.fullDescription: South Korea enacted strict anti-espionage measures for national strategic technologies. The penalty for stealing semiconductor, battery, or display trade secrets to foreign entities was increased to up to 30 years imprisonment (2023 reform). Korea has documented numerous cases of Chinese entities attempting to acquire semiconductor technology from Samsung and SK Hynix through employee poaching and corporate espionage. The Industrial Technology Protection Act covers national core technologies.
laws.penalty: Trade secret theft to foreign entity: up to 30 years imprisonment (2023 reform); corporate violations: up to 2 billion won
exceptions: Legitimate technology licensing agreements
Academic publications on fundamental research

quiz.q: To how many years imprisonment was the penalty for stealing semiconductor trade secrets to foreign entities increased in South Korea in 2023?
quiz.explanation: In 2023, South Korea increased the maximum penalty for stealing national core technology trade secrets (including semiconductors, batteries, and displays) to foreign entities to up to 30 years imprisonment, reflecting the strategic importance of these industries.

laws.title: Nuclear Energy Act / Energy Transition Debate
laws.subtitle: Nuclear power and energy mix
laws.fullDescription: South Korea is highly nuclear-dependent (about 30% of electricity from nuclear plants). President Moon's government (2017-2022) pursued nuclear phase-out; President Yoon reversed this with a 'pro-nuclear' policy including new reactor construction and extending existing plants. Korea's APR-1400 reactor technology has been exported to the UAE (Barakah Nuclear Power Plant — built by KEPCO). The energy mix debate between nuclear, gas, and renewables is central to Korea's energy policy.
laws.penalty: Nuclear safety violations: NSSC orders; reactor operation without license: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Research reactors have different regulatory framework
Decommissioning activities under modified rules
laws.sourceLabel: Nuclear Safety and Security Commission Korea

quiz.q: To which country did South Korea export its APR-1400 nuclear reactor technology, completing a major nuclear construction project?
quiz.explanation: South Korea exported its APR-1400 reactor technology to the UAE, with the Barakah Nuclear Power Plant (built by Korea Electric Power Corporation/KEPCO) becoming the first operational nuclear power plant in the Arab world, starting operations in 2021.

laws.title: Birth Rate Policy / Childcare Law
laws.subtitle: Childcare support and parental leave
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has dramatically expanded childcare to address its birth rate crisis. Government-subsidized childcare (eorinee jib) is available for all children under 5. Parents can claim childcare tax credits. Parental leave is available to both parents but uptake by fathers is very low (cultural stigma). The government provides baby bonus payments (200만원 at birth, 月100만원 for 12 months). Despite unprecedented investment, birth rates continue to fall.
laws.penalty: Childcare center safety violations: license revocation; fraud in childcare subsidies: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Registered childcare centers receive subsidies
Employer-provided childcare facilities have tax incentives
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Health Welfare Korea Childcare

quiz.q: How long is the baby bonus monthly payment provided by the South Korean government after birth (as of 2024)?
quiz.explanation: As of 2024, South Korea provides a birth bonus of 2 million won, followed by 1 million won per month for 12 months, as part of the government's emergency measures to address its record-low birth rate.

laws.title: Sports Betting / Illegal Gambling
laws.subtitle: Sports betting and organized gambling crime
laws.fullDescription: Legal sports betting in South Korea is limited to specific government-run platforms (Toto, Proto for football). All other forms of sports betting are illegal but the illegal online gambling market (estimated over 80 trillion won annually) vastly exceeds legal channels. Sports match-fixing has been a significant concern — Korean football and baseball have had high-profile match-fixing scandals. Offshore online gambling remains technically illegal for Koreans.
laws.penalty: Illegal gambling operation: up to 5 years imprisonment; gambling: up to 3 years
exceptions: Horse racing, bicycle racing, and motorboat racing legal under licensed operators
Casinos legal for foreigners; Kangwon Land for Korean citizens

quiz.q: What is one legal casino in South Korea that Korean citizens (not just foreigners) are allowed to visit?
quiz.explanation: Kangwon Land is the only casino in South Korea where Korean citizens are legally permitted to gamble — all other Korean casinos are restricted to foreign visitors. Kangwon Land was established in 2000 to provide economic development in a former coal mining region.

laws.title: SKY Universities / College Admissions
laws.subtitle: Elite universities and meritocracy
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's college admissions system revolves around the SKY universities (Seoul National, Korea, Yonsei) — graduates of these institutions dominate government, law, medicine, and business. The college admissions process combines CSAT scores, school records, and interviews. Controversies around admission scandals (professors' children receiving special treatment) led to reforms. The Cho Kuk scandal (2019-2020) — involving a justice minister candidate whose daughter allegedly received fraudulent academic qualifications — sparked massive protests.
laws.penalty: Academic fraud in university admissions: criminal prosecution; university sanctions
exceptions: Special admission quotas for athletes, artists, and disadvantaged students
Rural university admission preferences

quiz.q: What do the letters 'SKY' stand for in the context of South Korean universities?
quiz.explanation: 'SKY' refers to the three most prestigious universities in South Korea: Seoul National University (S), Korea University (K), and Yonsei University (Y). These institutions' graduates dominate the highest levels of Korean government, law, business, and medicine.

laws.title: Overseas Resources Development / KORES
laws.subtitle: Resource security and overseas investment
laws.fullDescription: South Korea is highly resource-dependent (imports virtually all oil, gas, and coal). The Korea Resources Corporation (KORES) and Korea National Oil Corporation (KNOC) make overseas resource investments. A series of unsuccessful overseas resource investments under the Lee Myung-bak administration (2008-2013) cost the public approximately 40 trillion won, leading to investigations and prosecutions. Korea is a major LNG buyer globally.
laws.penalty: Misappropriation of public funds in overseas investment: criminal prosecution
exceptions: Private energy company investments follow commercial rules
Strategic petroleum reserve management

quiz.q: Approximately how much did South Korea's overseas resource investment failures under the Lee Myung-bak administration cost?
quiz.explanation: A series of disastrous overseas resource investments made by state companies during the Lee Myung-bak administration (2008-2013) are estimated to have cost approximately 40 trillion won of public funds, leading to investigations and prosecution of officials involved.

laws.title: Freedom of Assembly Act / Protest Law
laws.subtitle: Right to protest and assembly restrictions
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's Assembly and Demonstration Act regulates protests. Large labor protests by the KCTU and FKTU regularly occur in Seoul — candlelight rallies are a distinctive tradition (used against Park Geun-hye and US beef imports). Police use water cannons and pepper spray in some demonstrations. Night protests in residential areas can be restricted. The Yoon government prosecuted KCTU leader Yang Kyung-su for organizing an illegal assembly, raising concerns about assembly rights.
laws.penalty: Illegal assembly organization: up to 3 years imprisonment; blocking traffic: separate traffic offenses
exceptions: Spontaneous assemblies have some protection
Religious gatherings and cultural events have lighter requirements

quiz.q: What distinctive form of protest has become a Korean tradition, used notably against President Park Geun-hye?
quiz.explanation: Candlelight vigils and rallies (촛불집회) have become a distinctive form of South Korean protest — used memorably in 2002 (after US military vehicle accident), 2008 (US beef imports), and most famously in 2016-17 against President Park Geun-hye's corruption, eventually leading to her impeachment.

laws.title: Population Crisis Policy
laws.subtitle: Birth Rate Emergency Measures Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's total fertility rate hit 0.72 in 2023, the lowest ever recorded for any country. The government declared a demographic emergency and established the Ministry of Population Strategy (2023). Billions in incentives offer cash bonuses (up to 2 million KRW monthly), housing priority, and tax breaks for families with children. Critics argue structural issues—housing costs, education expenses, gender inequality, and work culture—cannot be fixed with cash payments.
laws.penalty: No individual penalties; government agencies face performance reviews for failing demographic targets.
exceptions: Incentives stack with local government programs
Foreign residents may qualify after 5 years of legal residency

quiz.q: What was South Korea's total fertility rate in 2023?
quiz.explanation: 0.72 is the lowest fertility rate ever recorded for any country, prompting South Korea to declare a demographic national emergency.

laws.title: Cybercrime Act
laws.subtitle: Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization and Information Protection
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's cyber law framework criminalizes unauthorized access, data breaches, malware distribution, and online fraud. The 2020 amendments strengthened penalties for ransomware attacks and corporate data theft. The Korea Internet & Security Agency (KISA) enforces cybersecurity standards. Notable cases include the 2014 Korea Credit Bureau breach (20 million records) leading to stricter financial data protection. Cross-border cybercrime is addressed via Interpol cooperation and bilateral treaties.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized access: up to 3 years imprisonment or 30 million KRW fine. Data breach causing harm: up to 5 years or 50 million KRW.
exceptions: Security researchers with prior written consent
Government-authorized penetration testing

quiz.q: Which government agency enforces cybersecurity standards in South Korea?
quiz.explanation: KISA (Korea Internet & Security Agency) is responsible for cybersecurity standards enforcement and incident response in South Korea.

laws.title: Constitutional Court Powers
laws.subtitle: Constitutional Court Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's Constitutional Court (헌법재판소), established in 1988, has sweeping powers: it can strike down laws as unconstitutional, adjudicate state power disputes, review constitutional complaints from individuals, and—critically—rule on presidential impeachment. The Court has two landmark impeachment rulings: Roh Moo-hyun (2004, restored to office) and Park Geun-hye (2017, removed). The 2024-2025 Yoon Suk-yeol impeachment case is pending before the Court. Justices serve 6-year terms.
laws.penalty: Court rulings are final and binding; no appeal mechanism exists. Laws struck down lose legal force immediately.
exceptions: President retains immunity from criminal prosecution while in office (except for treason/insurrection)
Court requires 6 of 9 justices to remove a president

quiz.q: How many justices must vote to remove a South Korean president via impeachment?
quiz.explanation: The Constitutional Court requires 6 of 9 justices to vote for removal to impeach a South Korean president. Park Geun-hye was removed 8-0 in 2017.

laws.title: Fine Dust Air Quality Law
laws.subtitle: Special Act on the Improvement of Air Quality in Indoor Air and Atmospheric Environment
laws.fullDescription: South Korea suffers severe fine dust (미세먼지/PM2.5) pollution, partly from domestic coal plants and partly from Chinese industrial emissions. The 2019 Special Act mandates emergency reduction measures when PM2.5 exceeds thresholds: odd-even vehicle restrictions, coal plant shutdowns, and school closures. The government set a 2030 target of 35% domestic emission reduction. Korea-China-Japan trilateral cooperation addresses transboundary pollution. Public dust masks became mandatory on high-pollution days.
laws.penalty: Industrial violators: fines up to 500 million KRW. Vehicle non-compliance during emergency: 100,000 KRW fine.
exceptions: Emergency and commercial vehicles exempt from odd-even restrictions
Certain industrial processes granted temporary exemptions

quiz.q: What vehicle restriction is imposed during South Korea's fine dust emergency days?
quiz.explanation: During fine dust emergencies, South Korea implements odd-even number plate restrictions, allowing only vehicles with odd or even plate numbers on alternating days.

laws.title: Drunk Driving Reform
laws.subtitle: 윤창호법 — Act Amending Road Traffic Act
laws.fullDescription: The 'Yoon Chang-ho Law' (2018) dramatically tightened drunk driving penalties after 22-year-old Yoon Chang-ho was killed by a repeat drunk driver. The BAC limit for driving under influence was lowered from 0.05% to 0.03%, and the threshold for license suspension dropped from 0.1% to 0.08%. Repeat offenders face up to 3 years imprisonment. Causing death while drunk driving carries up to life imprisonment. Public outrage over lenient sentences for repeat offenders drove swift legislative reform.
laws.penalty: DUI (0.03-0.08% BAC): license suspension, fine up to 5 million KRW. Above 0.08%: up to 1 year prison. Causing death: up to life imprisonment.
exceptions: Medical emergencies (driving to hospital)
Involuntary intoxication (extremely rare)

quiz.q: What BAC limit triggered the Yoon Chang-ho Law reform in South Korea?
quiz.explanation: The Yoon Chang-ho Law lowered the DUI BAC threshold from 0.05% to 0.03%, one of the strictest standards in Asia, following public outrage over a fatal drunk driving incident.

laws.title: Disability Rights Act
laws.subtitle: Act on the Prohibition of Discrimination against Persons with Disabilities
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's 2007 Disability Discrimination Act prohibits discrimination in employment, education, goods and services, and public facilities. The National Human Rights Commission investigates complaints. Employers with 50+ workers must meet a 3.1% disability employment quota or pay a levy. However, enforcement is criticized as weak—physical accessibility in older buildings remains poor, and disability poverty rates are high. The 2022 CRPD review noted persistent gaps in community living and deinstitutionalization.
laws.penalty: Employers failing quota: levy of approximately 1 million KRW per unfilled position per month. Discrimination: damages and correction orders.
exceptions: Small businesses (under 50 employees) exempt from quota
Reasonable accommodation may be waived if undue hardship proven

quiz.q: What disability employment quota must South Korean employers with 50+ workers meet?
quiz.explanation: South Korean employers with 50 or more workers must employ at least 3.1% persons with disabilities or pay a monthly levy per unfilled position.

laws.title: Industrial Espionage Law
laws.subtitle: Act on Prevention of Divulgence and Protection of Industrial Technology
laws.fullDescription: South Korea treats semiconductor and display technology theft as a national security matter. The 2022 amendment classified certain technologies (Samsung DRAM, SK Hynix HBM, LG OLED) as 'National Core Technologies' requiring government approval before foreign transfer. Penalties were raised to 15 years imprisonment for overseas leakage. The law targets Chinese recruitment of Korean engineers—dozens of cases prosecuted annually. The Korea Trade Commission and National Intelligence Service jointly investigate cases. Samsung, SK Hynix, and LG file dozens of complaints per year.
laws.penalty: Overseas technology leakage: up to 15 years imprisonment and 1.5 billion KRW fine. Domestic leakage: up to 10 years.
exceptions: Licensed technology transfers with MOTIE approval
Academic research collaborations under official MOUs

quiz.q: How many years imprisonment can South Korea impose for overseas leakage of National Core Technologies?
quiz.explanation: The 2022 amendment raised the penalty for overseas leakage of National Core Technologies (like Samsung DRAM or SK Hynix HBM chips) to up to 15 years imprisonment.

laws.title: Nuclear Energy Policy
laws.subtitle: Nuclear Energy Promotion Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea generates about 30% of its electricity from 26 nuclear reactors. The Moon Jae-in administration (2017-2022) pursued a phase-out policy, canceling new plants and accelerating retirements. President Yoon Suk-yeol reversed course (2022), pledging to expand nuclear to 30%+ of the energy mix and extend reactor lifetimes. South Korea exports reactor technology (APR-1400) to UAE (Barakah plant). Nuclear waste storage remains contentious with no permanent repository. The 2023 energy plan targets 33% nuclear by 2030.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed nuclear activities: criminal prosecution under Nuclear Safety Act. Regulatory violations: shutdown orders and fines up to 200 million KRW.
exceptions: Research reactors at universities operate under separate licensing
Medical and industrial isotope use under NSSC permits

quiz.q: What percentage of South Korea's electricity currently comes from nuclear power?
quiz.explanation: South Korea generates approximately 30% of its electricity from 26 nuclear reactors, with government plans to increase this to 33% by 2030 under the Yoon administration's pro-nuclear policy.

laws.title: Childcare and Birth Bonus Policy
laws.subtitle: Infant Care Act and Population Basic Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea offers an escalating set of birth incentives to combat its record-low fertility rate. As of 2024: a 2 million KRW 'baby box' at birth, monthly allowances of 700,000 KRW for infants (age 0-11), parental leave of up to 1 year each parent (52 weeks), and priority public housing access. Local governments add their own bonuses—some rural areas offer up to 10 million KRW for a third child. Despite spending over $200 billion on pro-natalist policies since 2006, fertility continues to fall, raising questions about fundamental structural barriers.
laws.penalty: Employers denying parental leave: fines up to 5 million KRW. False claims for baby bonuses: repayment plus penalties.
exceptions: Freelancers and self-employed have reduced parental leave entitlements
Foreign residents may qualify for some benefits after 1 year of legal residency

quiz.q: Approximately how much has South Korea spent on pro-natalist policies since 2006?
quiz.explanation: South Korea has spent over $200 billion on pro-natalist policies since 2006, yet fertility rates have continued to fall, reaching a record low of 0.72 in 2023.

laws.title: Sports Gambling and Match-Fixing Law
laws.subtitle: National Sports Promotion Act
laws.fullDescription: Legal sports betting in South Korea is tightly controlled: only government-run Sports Toto (토토) is legal, offering fixed-odds betting on soccer, basketball, and baseball. Private or offshore gambling sites are illegal. The 2011 K-League match-fixing scandal led to life bans for dozens of players and stricter regulations. The 2015 amendment criminalized offering or accepting bribes to fix sporting outcomes. Professional athletes and officials are prohibited from gambling on their own sports. Online illegal gambling is estimated at several trillion KRW annually.
laws.penalty: Match-fixing: up to 5 years imprisonment or 50 million KRW fine. Illegal gambling: up to 3 years or 20 million KRW. Operating illegal betting sites: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Licensed Sports Toto purchases are legal
Casinos for foreigners (like Paradise Casino) are permitted

quiz.q: What is the only legal sports betting platform in South Korea?
quiz.explanation: Sports Toto (토토) is the only government-authorized sports betting platform in South Korea. All private, offshore, or unlicensed sports gambling is illegal.

laws.title: Chaebol Tax and Inheritance
laws.subtitle: Inheritance Tax Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has one of the world's highest inheritance tax rates—maximum 50%, rising to 60% for largest shareholders. This creates extraordinary burdens for chaebol succession: Samsung's Lee family faced an estimated 12 trillion KRW ($9 billion) inheritance tax bill after Lee Kun-hee's 2020 death, requiring asset sales and charitable donations. Critics argue high rates force family owners to pledge shares as collateral and maintain control through complex circular ownership structures rather than direct shareholding. Reform debates have stalled.
laws.penalty: Non-payment of inheritance tax: seizure of assets, additional penalties of 10-40% of owed amount, potential criminal prosecution for tax evasion.
exceptions: Charitable donations to approved foundations reduce taxable estate
Installment payment plans available (up to 5 years)

quiz.q: What was the approximate inheritance tax bill faced by Samsung's Lee family after Lee Kun-hee's 2020 death?
quiz.explanation: Samsung's Lee family faced an estimated 12 trillion KRW (approximately $9 billion) inheritance tax bill following Lee Kun-hee's death in 2020, forcing asset sales and major charitable donations.

laws.title: E-Commerce and Platform Regulation
laws.subtitle: Act on Consumer Protection in Electronic Commerce
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's e-commerce market is among the world's largest per capita, dominated by Coupang (로켓배송/Rocket Delivery), Naver Shopping, and Kakao Commerce. The 2021 Online Platform Competition Promotion Act proposed antitrust rules for dominant platforms but has faced industry opposition. Coupang's fulfillment center fire (2021) killed a firefighter and sparked warehouse safety regulations. The 2023 e-commerce consumer protection rules require faster refund processing and prohibit dark patterns. Delivery workers' labor protections are debated following multiple overwork deaths.
laws.penalty: Consumer protection violations: fines up to 100 million KRW. Deceptive advertising: up to 3 years or 30 million KRW fine.
exceptions: Small sellers below revenue thresholds face reduced compliance requirements
Cross-border purchases under personal use limits have simplified customs

quiz.q: Which South Korean company operates the 'Rocket Delivery' (로켓배송) same-day delivery service?
quiz.explanation: Coupang operates 로켓배송 (Rocket Delivery), South Korea's dominant same-day and next-day e-commerce delivery service, capturing a large share of the country's massive e-commerce market.

laws.title: Criminal Defamation Law
laws.subtitle: Criminal Act Articles 307-309
laws.fullDescription: Unlike most democracies, South Korea criminalizes defamation even when the statement is TRUE. Article 307 punishes false statements; Article 309 adds aggravation for media distribution. Article 310 provides a truth defense only when the statement serves 'solely the public interest'—a narrow exception. Journalists, bloggers, and even ordinary citizens face prosecution for exposing corruption if the subject pursues criminal charges. The law has been used to silence whistleblowers and investigative reporters. The UN Human Rights Committee has called for its repeal.
laws.penalty: Defamation with false facts (media): up to 7 years imprisonment or 50 million KRW. Defamation with true facts: up to 2 years or 5 million KRW.
exceptions: Statements purely in public interest with no private motive may invoke Article 310 defense
Parliamentary immunity for statements made in National Assembly

quiz.q: What makes South Korea's defamation law unusual compared to most democracies?
options: True statements can still be criminally prosecuted
Only politicians can file defamation cases
Defamation is only a civil matter
quiz.explanation: South Korea criminalizes defamation even when the statement is TRUE. Article 307 of the Criminal Act allows prosecution for true defamatory statements, with the public interest defense (Article 310) interpreted very narrowly.

laws.title: Urban Planning and Seoul Megacity Law
laws.subtitle: National Land Planning and Utilization Act
laws.fullDescription: Seoul and its satellite cities form one of the world's largest urban agglomerations (25+ million). The National Land Planning Act governs land use zoning, development permits, and urban renewal. The Gangnam district's development (1970s-1980s) created extreme real estate inequality. Recent policies include 3rd New Town (3기 신도시) construction to add 300,000 housing units and the 'Seoul to Sejong' administrative capital relocation (partially implemented). Green belt (개발제한구역) regulations strictly limit suburban sprawl but are frequently adjusted under political pressure.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized development: demolition orders, fines up to 500 million KRW. Zoning violations: construction halts and restoration requirements.
exceptions: Agricultural land in green belt zones has limited exemptions for farmers
Infrastructure projects with national designation can override green belt limits

quiz.q: Approximately how many people live in the greater Seoul metropolitan area?
quiz.explanation: The Seoul metropolitan area, including satellite cities like Incheon, Suwon, and Seongnam, houses over 25 million people, making it one of the world's largest urban agglomerations and home to about half of South Korea's total population.

laws.title: Bioethics and Hwang Woo-suk Scandal
laws.subtitle: Bioethics and Safety Act
laws.fullDescription: The 2005 Hwang Woo-suk scandal shook global science: Hwang, celebrated as a national hero for claimed breakthroughs in human embryonic stem cells and cloning, was exposed as having fabricated data in his landmark Science papers. He was convicted of fraud and misappropriation of research funds. The scandal led to South Korea enacting strict bioethics laws regulating human embryo research, cloning, and genetic testing. The Bioethics and Safety Act (2004, substantially amended 2012) requires IRB approval for all human subject research and prohibits reproductive human cloning.
laws.penalty: Reproductive human cloning: up to 10 years imprisonment. Research ethics violations: loss of funding, institutional sanctions, and potential criminal charges.
exceptions: Therapeutic cloning research with strict oversight is permitted under specific conditions
Somatic cell nuclear transfer for stem cell research allowed with MFDS approval

quiz.q: What crime was South Korean scientist Hwang Woo-suk convicted of following the 2005 scandal?
quiz.explanation: Hwang Woo-suk was convicted of research fraud (fabricating stem cell and cloning data published in Science) and misappropriation of research funds, and the scandal spurred South Korea's strict Bioethics and Safety Act.

laws.title: Elderly Poverty and Welfare Law
laws.subtitle: Welfare of Older Persons Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has one of the highest elderly poverty rates among OECD nations (about 40% of those over 66 live in relative poverty).
