The Basic Old-Age Pension provides about 300,000 KRW/month to qualifying seniors, far below living costs. Confucian traditions of family care are breaking down as urbanization separates families. The National Pension System (NPS), started in 1988, won't reach maturity until 2040s. Senior employment rates are high but mostly in precarious low-wage jobs. Elderly suicide rates are among the world's highest.
laws.penalty: Abandonment or neglect of elderly family members: up to 5 years imprisonment under Elder Welfare Act.
exceptions: Basic Old-Age Pension means-tested; upper-income seniors excluded
Long-term care insurance covers home care or facility care for those rated by assessment

quiz.q: What percentage of South Koreans over 66 live in relative poverty?
quiz.explanation: Approximately 40% of South Koreans over 66 live in relative poverty, one of the highest elderly poverty rates among OECD nations, despite significant government pension and welfare spending.

laws.title: Internet Real-Name System
laws.subtitle: Act on Promotion of Information and Communications Network Utilization
laws.fullDescription: South Korea attempted mandatory internet real-name verification (인터넷 실명제) from 2007: major websites had to verify users' national ID before allowing comments. The Constitutional Court struck it down in 2012 as unconstitutional—violating freedom of expression and privacy by chilling anonymous speech. A narrower form survived for election-period political ads. The ruling acknowledged that anonymity enables minority voices and dissent. South Korea still requires identity verification for SIM cards, financial services, and government portals, but not for general internet commenting.
laws.penalty: Pre-2012: platforms violating real-name rules faced fines. Post-ruling: real-name requirements for comments are unconstitutional; SIM and financial ID rules remain.
exceptions: Government services (G4C, HIRA, etc.) still require national ID verification
Campaign advertising during elections requires real-name disclosure

quiz.q: In what year did South Korea's Constitutional Court strike down mandatory internet real-name verification for commenting?
quiz.explanation: In 2012, South Korea's Constitutional Court struck down the mandatory internet real-name system introduced in 2007, ruling it unconstitutional for chilling freedom of expression and violating privacy rights.

laws.title: National Health Insurance Universality
laws.subtitle: National Health Insurance Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea achieved universal health insurance coverage in 1989 through the National Health Insurance Service (NHIS). All residents—employees, self-employed, and dependents—are covered. Premium contributions are income-based for employees (about 7% of salary, split employer/employee) and property/income-based for the self-employed. The single-payer NHIS negotiates fees with providers, keeping costs relatively low. South Korea's health outcomes (life expectancy 83+) and efficiency are world-class. Foreigners staying 6+ months must enroll.
laws.penalty: Failure to enroll: premium surcharges and back-payment requirements. Premium non-payment: wage garnishment and benefit suspension.
exceptions: Short-term visitors (under 6 months) may opt out
Diplomatic personnel exempt under Vienna Convention

quiz.q: In what year did South Korea achieve universal health insurance coverage?
quiz.explanation: South Korea achieved universal health insurance coverage in 1989, when the National Health Insurance system was expanded to cover all residents, becoming a model for single-payer systems worldwide.

laws.title: Drug Control and Zero Tolerance
laws.subtitle: Act on the Control of Narcotics
laws.fullDescription: South Korea maintains strict zero-tolerance drug policies. Cannabis is fully illegal—even if consumed legally abroad, returning Koreans can be prosecuted. Possession of any amount of marijuana carries up to 5 years. The 2023 wave of celebrity drug scandals (Yoo Ah-in, others) sparked renewed enforcement. Methamphetamine (필로폰) carries up to life imprisonment for trafficking. Hair follicle tests are used to prosecute overseas consumption. International drug-related organized crime falls under INTERPOL cooperation. Drug courts offer treatment diversion for first-time offenders.
laws.penalty: Cannabis possession: up to 5 years or 50 million KRW. Methamphetamine trafficking: up to life imprisonment. Overseas consumption punishable upon return.
exceptions: Prescribed medications with controlled substances legal with valid prescription
CBD products in strictly regulated medical contexts (very limited)

quiz.q: Can South Koreans who legally consume cannabis abroad be prosecuted upon returning home?
options: No, only domestic use is prosecuted
Only if they bring cannabis back
quiz.explanation: South Korea's zero-tolerance drug policy has extraterritorial reach: Koreans who legally consume cannabis in places like Canada or the United States can still be prosecuted under Korean law when they return home.

laws.title: THAAD Deployment and US Alliance
laws.subtitle: Republic of Korea-United States Mutual Defense Treaty
laws.fullDescription: The 1953 ROK-US Mutual Defense Treaty underpins the US military presence in South Korea (28,500 troops). The 2016-2017 deployment of THAAD (Terminal High Altitude Area Defense) missile batteries caused a severe diplomatic and economic crisis with China, which imposed informal trade sanctions (tourism bans, Lotte boycotts, K-pop restrictions) costing Korea an estimated $15 billion. The alliance includes burden-sharing negotiations (방위비분담금) that have been contentious. Combined Forces Command maintains wartime operational control (OPCON), which Korea seeks to regain.
laws.penalty: No domestic penalties; violations of Status of Forces Agreement (SOFA) by US personnel handled under agreed judicial procedures.
exceptions: SOFA gives US military personnel certain jurisdictional protections
Criminal cases involving serious crimes (murder, rape) transferred to Korean jurisdiction after 2001 revision

quiz.q: Approximately how much did China's informal economic retaliation over THAAD deployment cost South Korea?
quiz.explanation: China's informal economic retaliation against South Korea's THAAD deployment (2016-2017) cost an estimated $15 billion through tourism bans, Lotte boycott, and restrictions on Korean cultural exports to China.

laws.title: Candlelight Protests and Assembly Law
laws.subtitle: Assembly and Demonstration Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has a strong tradition of mass protest (촛불집회/candlelight vigils). The 2016-2017 candlelight protests that ousted President Park Geun-hye were the largest peaceful demonstrations in Korean history—up to 2 million participants weekly. The Assembly and Demonstration Act requires prior notification for demonstrations but prohibits banning them except for narrow national security grounds. Courts have ruled many police dispersals unconstitutional. The 2022 police use of water cannons and pepper spray against union protests drew criticism. Night demonstrations near the presidential residence remain restricted.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized assembly: up to 90 days detention or 1 million KRW fine. Violent demonstration: up to 5 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Spontaneous assemblies responding to sudden events may proceed without prior notification
Labor union actions during collective bargaining have some additional protections

quiz.q: Approximately how many people participated in the peak weekly candlelight protests against President Park Geun-hye?
quiz.explanation: At their peak in late 2016, the candlelight vigil protests against President Park Geun-hye drew up to 2 million participants per week in Seoul alone, becoming the largest peaceful demonstrations in South Korean history.

laws.title: Labor Union Rights and Disputes
laws.subtitle: Trade Union and Labor Relations Adjustment Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has a contentious labor relations system with two major union federations: KCTU (Korean Confederation of Trade Unions, more militant) and FKTU (Federation of Korean Trade Unions). The three-party Economic, Social and Labor Council (경제사회노동위원회) coordinates policy. The 2021 amendment expanded union rights for special employment workers (delivery drivers, platform workers). The 2022-2023 truckers' strike and cargo workers' dispute over minimum freight rates (안전운임제) led to confrontations and the government invoking emergency return-to-work orders.
laws.penalty: Illegal strikes: union leaders may face criminal prosecution for obstruction of business. Employers engaging in unfair labor practices: fines and orders to reinstate workers.
exceptions: Essential service workers (hospitals, utilities) face strike restrictions
Public sector unions prohibited from certain types of industrial action

quiz.q: What are the two major national labor union federations in South Korea?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's two major national labor union federations are the KCTU (Korean Confederation of Trade Unions), known for more militant stances, and the FKTU (Federation of Korean Trade Unions), generally more moderate.

laws.title: Higher Education and University Rankings
laws.subtitle: Higher Education Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's higher education system is highly stratified. SKY universities (Seoul National University, Korea University, Yonsei University) are considered the gateway to elite careers. University admission rates from top high schools determine social mobility. The government has tried to reduce university hierarchy through blind recruitment policies (blinding candidate university names on applications) and expanded vocational training. However, SKY brand power persists in chaebol hiring. The 2023 university reform required struggling provincial universities to merge or close as enrollment declines due to the demographic crisis.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent university applications: criminal prosecution for fraud, degree revocation. Academic credential falsification: up to 5 years for public officials.
exceptions: Transfer students and graduate school applicants follow different procedures
Foreign universities' Korean campuses (NYU Abu Dhabi model) have special status

quiz.q: What does the acronym 'SKY' represent in South Korean higher education?
quiz.explanation: SKY refers to South Korea's three most prestigious universities: Seoul National University (S), Korea University (K), and Yonsei University (Y). Admission to SKY schools is widely seen as essential for entry into elite chaebol companies and government positions.

laws.title: 1997 Financial Crisis Legacy Law
laws.subtitle: Financial Investment Services and Capital Markets Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's 1997 IMF crisis (외환위기/currency crisis) caused GDP to fall 5.8%, unemployment to double, and required a $57 billion IMF bailout. The crisis led to sweeping reforms: chaebol restructuring (the Big Deal mergers), banking sector consolidation, and the Capital Markets Act (2009) overhauling securities regulation. Korea repaid the IMF loan early (2001). The crisis created lasting economic trauma—Koreans donated gold jewelry to help repay national debt. Financial reform laws now require stricter corporate governance, consolidated supervision under the FSC/FSS, and foreign exchange liquidity management.
laws.penalty: Market manipulation: up to 10 years imprisonment. Insider trading: disgorgement plus fines up to 3x profits. Bank failures: KDIC insurance covers deposits up to 50 million KRW.
exceptions: KDIC deposit insurance covers per depositor per institution
Sovereign wealth fund (KIC) and foreign reserve management have separate governance

quiz.q: What triggered South Korea's 1997 financial crisis that required a $57 billion IMF bailout?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's 1997 crisis was triggered by a currency crisis combined with severely overleveraged chaebol conglomerates borrowing in foreign currencies. The won collapsed, requiring a $57 billion IMF bailout and triggering mass unemployment and corporate bankruptcies.

laws.title: AI and Deepfake Legislation
laws.subtitle: Act on Special Cases Concerning the Punishment of Sexual Crimes (AI Amendments)
laws.fullDescription: South Korea enacted some of the world's first AI-specific laws targeting deepfake crimes. The 2020 amendment criminalized non-consensual deepfake pornography—the direct legislative response to the N번방 Telegram sex crime network. The 2023 amendments banned election deepfakes within 90 days of voting. Korea's AI Basic Act (2023) passed, establishing a risk-based framework for AI governance similar to the EU AI Act but with lighter obligations. PIPC (Personal Information Protection Commission) investigates AI-generated data misuse.
laws.penalty: Distributing deepfake sexual content: up to 5 years imprisonment or 50 million KRW fine. Election deepfakes: up to 7 years.
exceptions: Satire and clearly marked parody may be exempt from election deepfake rules
Academic AI research with proper data ethics approval

quiz.q: What crime network directly prompted South Korea's 2020 deepfake pornography criminalization law?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's 2020 amendment criminalizing non-consensual deepfake pornography was a direct legislative response to the N번방 (Nth Room) Telegram sex crime network, which distributed non-consensual sexual material to hundreds of thousands of subscribers.

laws.title: Election Law and Campaign Finance
laws.subtitle: Public Official Election Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's election law is extremely strict. Campaign periods are legally limited: presidential races allow 23 days, National Assembly 13 days. Outdoor banners, door-to-door canvassing, and phone calls face specific time restrictions. The 2020 amendment introduced proportional representation mixed-member system (준연동형 비례대표제) for National Assembly elections. Political donations are capped and publicly disclosed. The NEC (National Election Commission) operates with constitutional independence. Election law violations by candidates can void their election even after winning.
laws.penalty: Vote-buying: up to 5 years imprisonment or 10 million KRW. Campaign finance violations: criminal prosecution and potential seat forfeiture.
exceptions: Internet campaign activities (SNS, blogs) permitted throughout the year
Official party activities outside designated campaign period allowed

quiz.q: How long is the legally permitted presidential campaign period in South Korea?
quiz.explanation: South Korea legally limits presidential campaign periods to just 23 days, one of the shortest in any democracy. National Assembly campaigns are limited to 13 days. Violations can result in criminal prosecution and seat forfeiture.

laws.title: Construction and Subcontracting Law
laws.subtitle: Framework Act on the Construction Industry
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's construction industry is dominated by chaebol-affiliated construction arms (Samsung C&T, Hyundai E&C, GS Construction). Multi-layered subcontracting—where main contractors hire sub-contractors who hire sub-sub-contractors—creates accountability gaps. Workers at the bottom are often underpaid or unpaid when a chain fails. The 2021 amendments strengthened protections: direct payment orders to subcontractors, criminal liability for non-payment, and wage escrow requirements for public projects. The 2022 Gwangju building collapse (17 killed) exposed regulatory failures in demolition practices.
laws.penalty: Subcontractor wage non-payment: up to 3 years imprisonment. Illegal subcontracting beyond permitted tiers: fines up to 30 million KRW.
exceptions: Specialty trades (electrical, plumbing) may subcontract under specific licenses
Design-build contracts have different subcontracting notification requirements

quiz.q: What 2022 accident exposed regulatory failures in South Korea's construction demolition practices?
quiz.explanation: The 2022 Gwangju building collapse killed 17 people, including passengers on a passing bus when a building under demolition collapsed onto the street, exposing serious regulatory and oversight failures in South Korea's construction demolition practices.

laws.title: Film Ratings and Content Regulation
laws.subtitle: Film and Video Rating Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's Media Rating Board (영상물등급위원회/KMRB) rates films and video content. Ratings: All, 12+, 15+, 18+, and Restricted (for venues only). The 2016 'Spirits' Busan International Film Festival government interference case tested film censorship limits when the government pressured BIFF to exclude a documentary critical of the Sewol ferry disaster response. Courts ruled the interference unconstitutional. North Korea-sympathetic content may be restricted under the National Security Act. Streaming platforms (Netflix, Wavve) follow same rating framework.
laws.penalty: Distributing unrated content: fines up to 30 million KRW. Distributing restricted content to minors: up to 3 years or 20 million KRW.
exceptions: Short films (under 60 minutes) screened at non-commercial venues may apply for exemption
Academic film screenings at universities are exempt from commercial rating requirements

quiz.q: What controversial 2016 case tested film censorship limits in South Korea?
options: Government interference at BIFF over Sewol documentary
quiz.explanation: In 2016, the South Korean government pressured the Busan International Film Festival (BIFF) to exclude a documentary critical of the government's Sewol ferry disaster response, and courts subsequently ruled this interference unconstitutional.

laws.title: Platform Worker Rights
laws.subtitle: Act on Protection of Persons Engaged in Special Types of Employment
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's gig economy is massive: Coupang, Baemin (food delivery), and Kakao T (ride-hailing) employ hundreds of thousands of platform workers classified as 'special employment type' (특수고용직) rather than employees. The 2021 law extended social insurance (industrial accident, employment insurance) to delivery riders and other platform workers. Baemin and Coupang Eats delivery riders can now claim workers' compensation. Kakao T driver disputes over algorithm-based dispatch led to legal challenges. The ILO has recommended full employee classification reforms.
laws.penalty: Platforms that misclassify workers to avoid insurance contributions: retroactive premium payments plus penalties up to 200% of unpaid contributions.
exceptions: True independent contractors (with multiple clients, own tools, set own hours) may retain contractor status
Short-term platform gigs below income thresholds have reduced contribution requirements

quiz.q: What 2021 reform extended industrial accident and employment insurance to South Korean platform workers?
options: Act on Protection of Special Employment Type Workers
quiz.explanation: The 2021 Act on Protection of Persons Engaged in Special Types of Employment extended social insurance including industrial accident and employment insurance to delivery riders, platform workers, and other 'special employment' workers in South Korea.

laws.title: Privacy and Surveillance Law
laws.subtitle: Personal Information Protection Act (PIPA) — Surveillance Provisions
laws.fullDescription: Beyond data protection, South Korea's surveillance legal framework is extensive. The National Intelligence Service (NIS) can intercept communications with court approval, and the Communications Protection Act governs wiretapping. The 2013 NIS scandal revealed illegal interference in the 2012 presidential election using social media manipulation—leading to NIS reform laws restricting domestic political activities. COVID-19 contact tracing used extensive CCTV, credit card, and mobile data—publicly disclosed per exposure notification regulations—raising privacy concerns. Korea has 3+ million CCTV cameras in public spaces.
laws.penalty: Illegal wiretapping: up to 10 years imprisonment. Unauthorized disclosure of intercepted communications: up to 7 years.
exceptions: Terrorism investigations allow extended surveillance periods under Anti-Terrorism Act
National security wiretaps approved by court have broader duration allowances

quiz.q: What 2013 NIS scandal led to reform laws restricting its domestic political activities?
quiz.explanation: In 2013, it was revealed that South Korea's National Intelligence Service (NIS) had illegally operated social media accounts to manipulate the 2012 presidential election, leading to criminal prosecutions and legal reforms restricting the NIS from domestic political activities.

laws.title: Korea-Japan Historical Disputes
laws.subtitle: 2015 Comfort Women Agreement and Forced Labor Rulings
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's courts have repeatedly clashed with Japan over colonial-era reparations. The 2018 Supreme Court ruling ordered Japanese companies (Nippon Steel, Mitsubishi) to compensate Korean forced labor victims—Japan called it a treaty violation of the 1965 normalization agreement. The 2015 comfort women agreement ('final and irreversible') was effectively nullified by the Moon government. A 2023 compromise (Yoon administration) created a Korean government fund to compensate victims, avoiding asset seizures of Japanese companies. Japan-Korea relations remain volatile, affecting security cooperation and trade.
laws.penalty: No domestic criminal penalties; Court-ordered compensation from Japanese companies can be enforced by seizing Korean assets of those companies.
exceptions: 1965 Treaty arguably settled government-to-government claims (Japan's position)
Individual victims' rights to sue remain contested under international law

quiz.q: What 2018 South Korean Supreme Court ruling escalated Japan-Korea historical tensions?
options: Ordered Japanese firms to compensate Korean forced labor victims
Ordered Japan to return colonial-era artifacts
Imposed visa restrictions on Japanese citizens
quiz.explanation: In 2018, South Korea's Supreme Court ordered Japanese companies including Nippon Steel and Mitsubishi to compensate Korean victims of forced wartime labor, which Japan rejected as a violation of the 1965 normalization agreement that settled colonial-era claims.

laws.title: Sports Law and Anti-Doping
laws.subtitle: Act on the Promotion of Sports and Support for Athletes
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's national sport obsession (기업 스포츠 체계/corporate sports system) means most professional athletes are employed by chaebols (Samsung Lions baseball, Hyundai Motorsport, etc.). The Korean Sport & Olympic Committee oversees athlete rights. The 2018 PyeongChang Winter Olympics spotlighted short-track speed skating team abuse—coaches were criminally prosecuted for physically and sexually abusing athletes. The 2020 Sports Ethics Center was established for abuse complaints. Anti-doping violations follow World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) standards with KADA (Korean Anti-Doping Agency) enforcement.
laws.penalty: Doping: 1-4 year competition ban per WADA code; criminal prosecution for trafficking performance-enhancing drugs.
exceptions: Therapeutic Use Exemptions (TUEs) for medical conditions with KADA approval
Athletes under 18 face reduced sanctions for first doping violations
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism

quiz.q: What 2018 PyeongChang Olympics scandal led to criminal prosecutions of coaches?
quiz.explanation: Following the 2018 PyeongChang Winter Olympics, South Korean short-track speed skating coaches were criminally prosecuted for systematic physical and sexual abuse of athletes, sparking major reforms and the creation of the Sports Ethics Center in 2020.

laws.title: Financial Services Regulation
laws.subtitle: Financial Services Commission Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's financial regulatory system uses a twin-peaks model: the Financial Services Commission (FSC) sets policy and the Financial Supervisory Service (FSS) supervises. Key areas: prudential regulation of banks, insurance, and securities; household debt management (which reached 105% of GDP—one of the world's highest); and cryptocurrency exchanges (required to register with FIU under SPCMLA). The 2023 Terra/LUNA cryptocurrency collapse (created by Korean Do Kwon) wiped $40 billion in global value and led to his prosecution and extradition. Virtual asset regulations tightened significantly.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed financial services: up to 5 years imprisonment or 50 million KRW. Market manipulation: up to 10 years.
exceptions: Sandbox regulatory exemptions for fintech startups (financial innovation act)
P2P lending platforms under 50 billion KRW have lighter requirements

quiz.q: What South Korean-founded cryptocurrency collapse in 2023 wiped $40 billion in global value?
quiz.explanation: The Terra/LUNA cryptocurrency ecosystem, created by Korean entrepreneur Do Kwon, collapsed in 2022-2023 (prosecution ongoing), wiping approximately $40 billion in global value and leading to major tightening of South Korea's cryptocurrency exchange regulations.

laws.title: Water Quality and Han River Protection
laws.subtitle: Water Environment Conservation Act
laws.fullDescription: The Han River running through Seoul is central to South Korea's water supply and recreation. The 4 Rivers Restoration Project (2009-2011, Lee Myung-bak administration) built 16 weirs and dredged major rivers at a cost of 22 trillion KRW. Environmental critics argued it worsened algae blooms; the Moon government partially dismantled some weirs. The Water Environment Conservation Act sets standards for effluent discharge, groundwater protection, and drinking water quality. Industrial pollution incidents (Samsung SDI chemical spill, etc.) trigger mandatory reporting and cleanup orders.
laws.penalty: Industrial effluent violations: fines up to 300 million KRW plus mandatory cleanup costs. Illegal discharge causing harm: criminal prosecution up to 7 years.
exceptions: Agricultural runoff faces lighter regulation than industrial discharge
Emergency bypasses during flood conditions may be permitted with notification

quiz.q: What was the cost of South Korea's controversial 4 Rivers Restoration Project (2009-2011)?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's 4 Rivers Restoration Project under President Lee Myung-bak cost 22 trillion KRW and built 16 weirs across the Han, Nakdong, Geum, and Yeongsan rivers. The project remains controversial, with critics arguing it worsened water quality rather than improving it.

laws.title: K-Pop Industry Regulation
laws.subtitle: Music Industry Promotion Act and Artist Contract Guidelines
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's K-pop industry generates billions in exports and significant soft power. The Fair Trade Commission (KFTC) regulates trainee and artist contracts after scandals over exploitative multi-year agreements. The 2009 TVXQ lawsuit against SM Entertainment exposed slave contract conditions (7 years, minimal pay). FTC guidelines now limit exclusive contracts to 7 years maximum and require minimum wage provisions. The 'school violence' disclosure system for idol candidates remains controversial. HYBE (BTS), SM, YG, and JYP are publicly traded companies subject to securities regulations.
laws.penalty: Contract violations against FTC guidelines: corrective orders and fines. Talent agency fraud (false promises): up to 3 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Joint ventures with foreign agencies may have different contract structures
Training period provisions in contracts may extend effective exclusive arrangements

quiz.q: What K-pop group's 2009 lawsuit against SM Entertainment exposed 'slave contract' conditions in the industry?
quiz.explanation: TVXQ's 2009 lawsuit against SM Entertainment exposed exploitative contract conditions—long terms (13+ years), minimal pay, and extreme restrictions—leading to FTC guidelines limiting exclusive artist contracts to 7 years maximum.

laws.title: Firearms Control Law
laws.subtitle: Act on the Safety Management of Guns, Swords, and Explosives
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has extremely strict firearms control. Private gun ownership is essentially prohibited except for hunters (long guns only, licensed and stored at police stations) and sports shooters (regulated facilities only). Police and military are the primary armed entities. South Korea has one of the world's lowest gun death rates (0.02 per 100,000, vs. US 12.21). The 2023 crossbow murder case prompted debate about regulating non-firearm weapons. Registered hunters must pass background checks, mental health screening, and complete 10 hours of training. Guns must be stored at designated police stations when not in active use.
laws.penalty: Unlicensed firearm possession: up to 5 years imprisonment or 20 million KRW. Armed robbery with firearm: up to 10 years or life.
exceptions: Licensed hunters permitted long guns stored at police stations
Sports shooting ranges operate under strict permit with on-site storage only

quiz.q: Where must licensed hunters in South Korea store their firearms when not actively hunting?
options: At home in a certified safe
quiz.explanation: South Korean gun law requires licensed hunters to store their firearms at designated police stations when not in active use, a key feature of South Korea's extremely strict gun control regime that results in one of the world's lowest gun death rates.

laws.title: Mental Health Policy
laws.subtitle: Mental Health Welfare Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea faces a mental health crisis: it has one of the OECD's highest suicide rates (approximately 25 per 100,000 annually). The 2016 Mental Health Welfare Act replaced the old law that permitted involuntary hospitalization without judicial oversight. The new law requires two psychiatrists to certify involuntary admission and mandates periodic review. Significant stigma around mental illness reduces treatment-seeking. Following celebrity suicides (SHINee's Jonghyun 2017, multiple others), social campaigns emerged. The 2021 COVID mental health impact intensified demand for counseling services.
laws.penalty: Illegal involuntary hospitalization: civil damages and administrative sanctions against facilities.
exceptions: Emergency involuntary admission permitted for immediate danger with 72-hour review
Guardians can consent for minors and severely incapacitated individuals

quiz.q: What reform did South Korea's 2016 Mental Health Welfare Act make to involuntary psychiatric hospitalization?
options: Required two psychiatrists plus periodic judicial review
Allowed family members to request hospitalization
quiz.explanation: South Korea's 2016 Mental Health Welfare Act replaced the old system allowing involuntary hospitalization without oversight; the new law requires certification from two psychiatrists and mandates periodic judicial review of continued involuntary confinement.

laws.title: Sewol Ferry Disaster and Safety Law
laws.subtitle: Act on Measures for the Improvement of Safety, etc. (Sewol Special Act)
laws.fullDescription: The April 2014 sinking of the MV Sewol killed 304 people, mostly high school students on a field trip to Jeju Island. The disaster exposed systemic failures: overloaded vessel, untrained crew who abandoned passengers, coast guard delays, and government communication failures. President Park Geun-hye's response during the crisis later became part of her impeachment case. The Sewol Special Act established the Truth and Safety Commission, mandated safety culture reforms across maritime and educational sectors, and funded a dedicated memorial. The ferry was salvaged in 2017.
laws.penalty: Dereliction of duty by crew: up to life imprisonment (captain sentenced to life). Coast guard officials: disciplinary action and criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Compensation fund established for victims and families through special legislation
Safety standards reforms apply phase-in periods for older vessels

quiz.q: How many people died in the 2014 MV Sewol sinking in South Korea?
quiz.explanation: The MV Sewol sinking on April 16, 2014 killed 304 people, the majority of whom were students from Danwon High School on a field trip. The disaster fundamentally changed South Korean attitudes toward government accountability and maritime safety.

laws.title: Police Reform Law
laws.subtitle: Police Act Amendment (2021 Detective Powers Transfer)
laws.fullDescription: A major 2021 reform transferred investigative authority from the Prosecution Service (검찰) to the police. Previously, prosecutors had near-total control of criminal investigations and indictments—creating extreme concentration of power. The reform gave police primary investigative authority and limited prosecutors to self-correction of police investigations. A new Investigation Headquarters (중대범죄수사청/Serious Crimes Investigation Agency) handles high-level corruption. Critics worry about lack of oversight of police investigative powers; reformers argued prosecutors had become a 'state within a state.'
laws.penalty: No direct penalties; structural reform affecting investigative jurisdiction. Police misconduct still subject to Corruption Investigation Office oversight.
exceptions: Prosecutors retain direct investigative authority for crimes involving prosecutors, judges, and senior officials
National security cases remain under NIS/joint investigative jurisdiction

quiz.q: What major change did South Korea's 2021 police reform make to the criminal investigation system?
options: Transferred primary investigative authority from prosecutors to police
Created a new federal police agency
Merged police and prosecutors into one agency
quiz.explanation: South Korea's 2021 reform transferred primary criminal investigative authority from the Prosecution Service to the police, ending prosecutors' near-total control of investigations and indictments that critics argued created dangerous concentrations of power.

laws.title: Multicultural Family Support Law
laws.subtitle: Multicultural Families Support Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has long been a homogeneous society but has seen rapid growth in multicultural families through international marriage (주로 Vietnamese, Chinese, Filipino spouses). The 2008 Multicultural Families Support Act provides Korean language education, cultural integration programs, and counseling for foreign spouses and their Korean-citizen children. As of 2023, about 1.1 million foreign residents live in Korea. Migrant workers (E-9 visa, EPS system) from Southeast Asia face documented exploitation and housing issues. The Marriage Migration Visa (F-6) requires sponsors to meet minimum income requirements.
laws.penalty: Domestic violence against multicultural family members: enhanced penalties under DV Act. Marriage fraud (sham marriages for visa): up to 3 years imprisonment.
exceptions: Humanitarian visa provisions for abused foreign spouses allow independent residency
Children of multicultural families have Korean citizenship by birth if one parent is Korean
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Gender Equality and Family

quiz.q: When was South Korea's Multicultural Families Support Act enacted?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's Multicultural Families Support Act was enacted in 2008, as the country began to see significant growth in international marriages and multicultural families, primarily involving Vietnamese, Chinese, and Filipino spouses of Korean nationals.

laws.title: Startup and Venture Capital Law
laws.subtitle: Special Measures Act for the Promotion of Venture Businesses
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's startup ecosystem has grown significantly from the 1990s Venture Bubble through to the current unicorn wave (Krafton, Kakao, Coupang, etc.). The Venture Business Promotion Act provides tax incentives, reduced regulatory burdens, and access to KOSDAQ (tech-focused exchange). The government's K-Startup initiative and Technology Guarantee Fund (KOTEC) provide loans and guarantees. Stock option rules were reformed in 2021 to allow broader employee participation. The startup-to-chaebol pipeline remains narrow, with many startups acquired by or dependent on chaebol networks.
laws.penalty: Fraudulent venture certification: loss of benefits plus repayment with 20% penalty. False financial statements: up to 10 years for securities fraud.
exceptions: Research-focused SMEs get additional R&D tax credits
Social enterprises with social value certification qualify for additional support programs

quiz.q: What is the name of South Korea's tech-focused stock exchange where many startups list?
quiz.explanation: KOSDAQ (Korea Securities Dealers Automated Quotations) is South Korea's tech-focused stock exchange, modeled after NASDAQ, where venture companies and startups can list with lower requirements than the main KOSPI market.

laws.title: Child Abuse and Protection Law
laws.subtitle: Child Abuse Crime Punishment Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's child protection system came under intense scrutiny after high-profile child abuse deaths: the 2020 'Jeong-in' case, where a 16-month-old died after repeated abuse by adoptive parents, shocked the nation. The Jeong-in Law (2021 amendment) mandated immediate separation of abused children, required police to accompany child protection workers on investigations, and strengthened penalties for parents and institutions. Child welfare institutions are required to conduct background checks and abuse training. Schools and medical providers are mandatory reporters.
laws.penalty: Child abuse causing death: up to life imprisonment (no parole). Physical child abuse: up to 10 years. Emotional abuse: up to 5 years.
exceptions: Reasonable disciplinary measures by parents (narrowly interpreted post-Jeong-in)
Foster parents who report abuse to authorities receive cooperation rather than prosecution

quiz.q: What 2020 case prompted South Korea's 'Jeong-in Law' strengthening child abuse protections?
options: Orphanage staff convicted of systemic abuse
Daycare CCTV footage of teacher abuse
quiz.explanation: The 2020 death of 16-month-old Jeong-in after repeated abuse by adoptive parents—who were initially not prosecuted despite medical red flags—shocked South Korea and prompted the 'Jeong-in Law' (2021), mandating immediate child separation and police accompaniment on abuse investigations.

laws.title: Maritime Law and Shipping Regulation
laws.subtitle: Marine Environment Management Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea is one of the world's largest shipbuilders (Hyundai Heavy Industries, Samsung Heavy Industries, DSME/Hanwha Ocean). Korean ships are subject to the Marine Pollution Prevention Act implementing MARPOL international conventions. The Hanjin Shipping bankruptcy (2016)—the world's 7th largest container line—caused global supply chain disruptions when 85 ships were stranded at sea, unable to unload. The fallout led to stricter financial monitoring of shipping companies. Port State Control inspections enforce international safety standards in Korean ports.
laws.penalty: Marine pollution violations: up to 5 years imprisonment or 50 million KRW. Falsification of pollution records: criminal prosecution.
exceptions: Vessels in distress (force majeure) may discharge limited pollutants to prevent total loss
Warships exempt from commercial environmental regulations (different MND standards)

quiz.q: What 2016 Korean shipping company bankruptcy caused global supply chain disruptions when 85 ships were stranded at sea?
quiz.explanation: Hanjin Shipping's 2016 bankruptcy—the world's 7th-largest container shipping line—stranded 85 vessels at sea and caused global supply chain disruptions, as ports refused to unload ships whose expenses could not be guaranteed, leading to billions in cargo losses worldwide.

laws.title: Public Housing and Rental Regulation
laws.subtitle: Rental Housing Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's unique jeonse (전세) system—where tenants pay a large deposit (typically 50-80% of property value) instead of monthly rent, with the deposit returned at lease end—has created systemic risk. The 2020-2022 jeonse crisis saw thousands of landlords unable to return deposits when property prices fell. The Jeonse Fraud Prevention Act (2023) established a registry of fraudulent landlords and deposit guarantee insurance. Public housing (LH Corporation) scandals involving insider land purchases (2021 LH scandal) devastated the housing agency's credibility and led to criminal prosecutions.
laws.penalty: Jeonse fraud (not returning deposit): civil enforcement plus criminal fraud prosecution, up to 10 years. LH insider trading: up to 7 years.
exceptions: Small landlords (one property, personal residence) have some extended return timeline allowances
Deposit insurance from KHFC covers up to 250 million KRW

quiz.q: What 2021 scandal devastated South Korea's state housing agency LH Corporation?
options: Insider land purchasing by LH employees
quiz.explanation: In 2021, it was revealed that hundreds of LH (Korea Land and Housing Corporation) employees had used their advance knowledge of government development plans to purchase land in the planned 3rd New Town areas, triggering mass public outrage, resignations, and criminal investigations.

laws.title: English Education and EFL Policy
laws.subtitle: English Program in Korea (EPIK) and Curriculum Act
laws.fullDescription: English proficiency is treated as essential for economic success in South Korea, creating a massive private English education industry (학원/hagwon). The government's EPIK (English Program in Korea) brings thousands of native English teachers annually from seven target countries (US, UK, Canada, Australia, NZ, Ireland, South Africa). From 2022, English became a mandatory subject from 3rd grade (previously 1st grade in some regions). Private English kindergartens faced prohibition under the Early Childhood Education Act (2014) to reduce inequality, but enforcement has been inconsistent.
laws.penalty: Operating unlicensed language institutes: fines up to 10 million KRW. False advertising of English education programs: KFTC enforcement actions.
exceptions: Foreign schools (Korean-American International School, etc.) may teach English-medium from earlier grades
International schools for foreign nationals follow different curriculum standards

quiz.q: What is the name of South Korea's government program that recruits native English speakers to teach in public schools?
quiz.explanation: EPIK (English Program in Korea) is the South Korean government's program that recruits native English-speaking teachers from seven target countries (including the US, UK, Canada, and Australia) to teach in public elementary, middle, and high schools nationwide.

laws.title: Violent Crime and Recidivism Law
laws.subtitle: Act on the Electronic Monitoring of Specific Criminal Offenders
laws.fullDescription: South Korea uses electronic ankle monitoring (전자발찌) for repeat violent and sex offenders. The law was expanded after high-profile recidivist crimes: the 2020 Gangnam stalking murder (victim killed while attacker had ankle monitor) and others highlighted monitoring failures. Electronic monitoring for sex offenders can extend 30 years post-sentence. The 2021 Stalking Punishment Act added emergency protective orders and criminalized stalking behavior. South Korea's overall violent crime rate is relatively low but repeat violent crime cases generate intense public concern.
laws.penalty: Violations of electronic monitoring conditions: up to 7 years imprisonment. Stalking: up to 5 years (aggravated if weapon used: up to 10 years).
exceptions: First-time offenders in non-violent crimes generally not subject to electronic monitoring
Medical hardship may result in suspension of monitoring requirements

quiz.q: For how long can sex offenders in South Korea be required to wear electronic ankle monitors post-sentence?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's electronic monitoring law for sex offenders allows ankle monitor requirements to extend up to 30 years after release from prison, one of the longest post-sentence monitoring periods in the world.

laws.title: Conscientious Objection and Military Service
laws.subtitle: Military Service Act — Conscientious Objection Ruling
laws.fullDescription: South Korea requires 18-21 months military service for all able-bodied men. For decades, conscientious objectors (primarily Jehovah's Witnesses) were imprisoned—over 19,000 served prison time since 1950. In 2018, the Constitutional Court ruled the lack of alternative service unconstitutional. The Alternative Service Act (2019) created a 36-month civilian service option (social welfare facilities, correctional institutions). The service is intentionally longer to prevent abuse. South Korea has imprisoned more conscientious objectors than any other country historically.
laws.penalty: Conscription evasion: up to 3 years imprisonment. Alternative service non-compliance: up to 1 year.
exceptions: Physical/mental disability qualifying under Military Manpower Administration standards
Overseas Korean nationals who acquire foreign citizenship before age 18 may be exempt

quiz.q: How long is South Korea's alternative civilian service option created for conscientious objectors?
quiz.explanation: South Korea's 2019 Alternative Service Act created a 36-month civilian service option (longer than the 18-21 month military service) for conscientious objectors, following a 2018 Constitutional Court ruling that the lack of any alternative was unconstitutional.

laws.title: Food Safety and Hygiene Law
laws.subtitle: Food Sanitation Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has comprehensive food safety regulation under the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety (MFDS). HACCP certification is mandatory for meat, dairy, and processed food factories. The 2017 salmonella egg crisis (following the European fipronil scandal), various kimchi lead contamination cases, and regular school lunch food poisoning incidents have driven stricter enforcement. School cafeteria inspections are mandatory. Food delivery platform meals (Baemin, Coupang Eats) face origin labeling requirements. Genetically modified food must be labeled if GM content exceeds 3%.
laws.penalty: Food adulteration: up to 10 years or 100 million KRW. False food labeling: up to 5 years or 50 million KRW. Repeated violations: business license revocation.
exceptions: Small-scale home food production for sale at markets has simplified registration
Traditional fermented foods (doenjang, kimchi) from certified traditional food businesses have heritage exemptions
laws.sourceLabel: Ministry of Food and Drug Safety

quiz.q: What percentage of GM content triggers mandatory labeling on food products in South Korea?
quiz.explanation: South Korea requires mandatory GMO labeling on food products when the genetically modified content exceeds 3% of the ingredient, bringing it in line with EU-style consumer transparency requirements for food genetic modification disclosure.

laws.title: Telecommunications Regulation
laws.subtitle: Telecommunications Business Act
laws.fullDescription: South Korea has world-leading broadband (average 100+ Mbps, 5G coverage over 90%). The three major telecom operators (SK Telecom, KT, LG U+) are regulated by the Korea Communications Commission (KCC) and Ministry of Science and ICT. The Mobile Virtual Network Operator (MVNO) market has expanded competition. Net neutrality principles were established in 2011 guidelines. The 2022 Netflix-SK Telecom dispute over network usage fees reached courts—reflecting global debates about who pays for streaming infrastructure. The 2023 KT ransomware attack exposed network infrastructure vulnerabilities.
laws.penalty: Unauthorized telecommunications services: up to 5 years or 200 million KRW. Network discrimination violations: fines up to 3% of annual revenue.
exceptions: MVNOs (budget carriers) operate under simplified licensing
Government emergency broadcast networks exempt from commercial fee structures

quiz.q: Which South Korean telecom dispute became a landmark case in the global debate over network usage fees for streaming services?
quiz.explanation: The Netflix vs SK Telecom/SK Broadband court dispute in 2022 became a landmark global case in the debate over whether streaming services should pay network usage fees to telecom providers for the infrastructure bandwidth they consume.

laws.title: Treason and Insurrection Law
laws.subtitle: Criminal Act Chapter 1 — Crimes of Insurrection and Foreign Aggression
laws.fullDescription: South Korea's insurrection law (내란죄) was thrust into the global spotlight in December 2024 when President Yoon Suk-yeol declared martial law, was rejected by the National Assembly within hours, and faced impeachment and criminal indictment for insurrection. Insurrection (내란) is one of only two crimes for which a sitting president has no immunity (the other being treason/외환죄). Yoon was arrested in January 2025—the first sitting South Korean president to be arrested. The Constitutional Court upheld his impeachment in 2025. Insurrection carries the death penalty or life imprisonment for leaders.
laws.penalty: Leaders of insurrection: death penalty or life imprisonment. Participants: up to 10 years imprisonment.
exceptions: No presidential immunity for insurrection and treason
Amnesty requires National Assembly approval and cannot cover insurrection leaders under most readings

quiz.q: What makes insurrection (내란죄) special under South Korean presidential immunity rules?
options: Presidents have no immunity for insurrection or treason
Insurrection is treated as a civil matter only
Only the National Assembly can prosecute insurrection
Insurrection charges require Supreme Court approval first
quiz.explanation: Insurrection (내란죄) and treason (외환죄) are the only two crimes for which the South Korean president has no immunity from criminal prosecution. This rule was invoked in the prosecution of President Yoon Suk-yeol following his December 2024 martial law declaration.
